 \amp= \det\mat{-\lambda, 6 8; \frac 12 -\lambda, 0; 0 \frac 12 -\lambda} \\
 \amp= 8\left(\frac 14 - 0\cdot-\lambda\right)
 - \lambda\left(\lambda^2 - 6\cdot\frac 12\right) \\
 \amp= -\lambda^3 + 3\lambda + 2.
 \end{split}$$

nodes.title: Eigenvalues are roots of the characteristic polynomial
nodes.body: Let $A$ be an $n\times n$ matrix, and let $f(\lambda) = \det(A-\lambda I_n)$ be its characteristic polynomial. Then a number $\lambda_0$ is an eigenvalue of $A$ if and only if $f(\lambda_0) = 0$.

nodes.title: Proof: Eigenvalues are roots of the characteristic polynomial
nodes.body:
By the [imt-2], the matrix equation $(A-\lambda_0 I_n)x=0$ has a nontrivial solution if and only if $\det(A-\lambda_0 I_n) = 0$. Therefore,

$$\begin{split}
 \lambda_0 \text{ is an eigenvalue of } A
 \amp\iff Ax = \lambda_0 x \text{ has a nontrivial solution} \\
 \amp\iff (A-\lambda_0 I_n)x = 0 \text{ has a nontrivial solution} \\
 \amp\iff A - \lambda_0 I_n \text{ is not invertible} \\
 \amp\iff \det(A - \lambda_0 I_n) = 0 \\
 \amp\iff f(\lambda_0) = 0.
 \end{split}$$

nodes.title: Finding eigenvalues
nodes.body:
Find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the matrix

$$A = \mat{5 2; 2 1}.$$

 In the above [charpoly-eg-22] we computed the characteristic polynomial of $A$ to be $f(\lambda) = \lambda^2-6\lambda + 1$. We can solve the equation $\lambda^2-6\lambda+1=0$ using the quadratic formula:

$$\lambda = \frac{6\pm\sqrt{36-4}}2 = 3\pm 2\sqrt 2.$$

 Therefore, the eigenvalues are $3+2\sqrt 2$ and $3-2\sqrt 2$.

 To compute the eigenvectors, we solve the homogeneous system of equations $(A-\lambda I_2)x=0$ for each eigenvalue $\lambda$. When $\lambda=3+2\sqrt 2$, we have

$$\begin{split}
 A-(3+\sqrt 2)I_2 = \amp\mat{2-2\sqrt2 2; 2 -2-2\sqrt2} \\
 \xrightarrow{R_1 = R_1\times(2+2\sqrt2)}\;
 \amp\mat{-4 4+4\sqrt2; 2 -2-2\sqrt2} \\
 \xrightarrow{R_2 = R_2+R_1/2}\;
 \amp\mat{-4 4+4\sqrt2; 0 0} \\
 \xrightarrow{R_1 = R_1 \div -4}\;
 \amp\mat{1 -1-\sqrt2; 0 0}.
 \end{split}$$

 The parametric form of the general solution is $x=(1+\sqrt 2)y$, so the $(3+2\sqrt 2)$-eigenspace is the line spanned by ${1+\sqrt 2\choose 1}$. We compute in the same way that the $(3-2\sqrt 2)$-eigenspace is the line spanned by ${1-\sqrt 2\choose 1}$.

 The green line is the $(3-2\sqrt 2)$-eigenspace, and the violet line is the $(3+2\sqrt 2)$-eigenspace.

nodes.title: Finding eigenvalues
nodes.body:
Find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the matrix

$$A = \mat{0 6 8; \frac 12 0 0; 0 \frac 12 0}.$$

 In the above [charpoly-eg-33] we computed the characteristic polynomial of $A$ to be $f(\lambda) = -\lambda^3+3\lambda+2$. We eyeball that $f(2) = -8 + 3\cdot 2 + 2 = 0$. Thus $\lambda-2$ divides $f(\lambda)$; to find the other roots, we perform polynomial long division:

$$\frac{-\lambda^3+3\lambda+2}{\lambda-2}
 = -\lambda^2-2\lambda-1 = -(\lambda+1)^2.$$

 Therefore,

$$f(\lambda) = -(\lambda-2)(\lambda+1)^2,$$

 so the only eigenvalues are $\lambda = 2,-1$.

 We compute the $2$-eigenspace by solving the homogeneous system $(A-2I_3)x=0$. We have

$$A-2I_3 = \mat{-2 6 8; \frac 12 -2 0; 0 \frac 12 -2}
 \quad\xrightarrow{\text{RREF}}\quad
 \mat{1 0 -16; 0 1 -4; 0 0 0}.$$

 The parametric form and parametric vector form of the solutions are:

$$\syseq{x = 16z; y = 4z; z = z}
 \quad\To\quad
 \vec{x y z} = z\vec{16 4 1}.$$

 Therefore, the $2$-eigenspace is the line

$$\Span\left\{\vec{16 4 1}\right\}.$$

 We compute the $-1$-eigenspace by solving the homogeneous system $(A+I_3)x=0$. We have

$$A+I_3 = \mat{1 6 8; \frac 12 1 0; 0 \frac 12 1}
 \quad\xrightarrow{\text{RREF}}\quad
 \mat{1 0 -4; 0 1 2; 0 0 0}.$$

 The parametric form and parametric vector form of the solutions are:

$$\syseq{x = 4z; y = -2z; z = z}
 \quad\To\quad
 \vec{x y z} = z\vec{4 -2 1}.$$

 Therefore, the $-1$-eigenspace is the line

$$\Span\left\{\vec{4 -2 1}\right\}.$$

 The green line is the $-1$-eigenspace, and the violet line is the $2$-eigenspace.

nodes.title: trace
charpoly-is-poly
nodes.body:
Let $A$ be an $n\times n$ matrix, and let $f(\lambda)=\det(A-\lambda I_n)$ be its characteristic polynomial. Then $f(\lambda)$ is a polynomial of degree $n$. Moreover, $f(\lambda)$ has the form

$$f(\lambda) = (-1)^n\lambda^n + (-1)^{n-1}\Tr(A)\lambda^{n-1} + \cdots + \det(A).$$

 In other words, the coefficient of $\lambda^{n-1}$ is $\pm\Tr(A)$, and the constant term is $\det(A)$ (the other coefficients are just numbers without names).

nodes.title: Proof: charpoly-is-poly
nodes.body:
First we notice that

$$f(0) = \det(A - 0I_n) = \det(A),$$

 so that the constant term is always $\det(A)$.

 We will prove the rest of the theorem only for $2\times 2$ matrices; the reader is encouraged to complete the proof in general using cofactor expansions. We can write a $2\times 2$ matrix as $A = \smallmat abcd$; then

$$\begin{split}
 f(\lambda) \amp= \det(A-\lambda I_2)
 = \det\mat{a-\lambda, b; c d-\lambda}
 = (a-\lambda)(d-\lambda)-bc \\
 \amp=\lambda^2 - (a+d)\lambda + (ad-bc)
 = \lambda^2 - \Tr(A)\lambda + \det(A).
 \end{split}$$

nodes.title: charpoly-example-5
nodes.body:
Find the characteristic polynomial of the matrix

$$A = \mat{5 2; 2 1}.$$

 We have

$$f(\lambda) = \lambda^2 - \Tr(A)\lambda + \det(A)
 = \lambda^2 - (5+1)\lambda + (5\cdot 1-2\cdot 2)
 = \lambda^2 - 6\lambda + 1,$$

 as in the above [charpoly-eg-22].

nodes.title: charpoly-remark-1
nodes.body: By the above [charpoly-is-poly], the characteristic polynomial of an $n\times n$ matrix is a polynomial of degree $n$. Since a polynomial of degree $n$ has at most $n$ roots, this gives another proof of the fact that an $n\times n$ matrix has at most $n$ eigenvalues. See this [evecs-max-nr].

nodes.title: charpoly-corollary-1
nodes.body: If $A$ is an upper- or lower-triangular matrix, then the eigenvalues of $A$ are its diagonal entries.

nodes.title: Proof: charpoly-corollary-1
nodes.body:
Suppose for simplicity that $A$ is a $3\times 3$ upper-triangular matrix:

$$A = \mat{a_{11} a_{12} a_{13}; 0 a_{22} a_{23}; 0 0 a_{33}}.$$

 Its characteristic polynomial is

$$f(\lambda) = \det(A-\lambda I_3)
 = \det\mat{a_{11}-\lambda, a_{12} a_{13};
 0 a_{22}-\lambda, a_{23};
 0 0 a_{33}-\lambda}.$$

 This is also an upper-triangular matrix, so the determinant is the product of the diagonal entries:

$$f(\lambda) = (a_{11}-\lambda)(a_{22}-\lambda)(a_{33}-\lambda).$$

 The zeros of this polynomial are exactly $a_{11},\,a_{22},\,a_{33}.$

nodes.title: charpoly-example-6
nodes.body:
Find the eigenvalues of the matrix

$$A = \mat{1 7 2 4; 0 1 3 11; 0 0 \pi, 101; 0 0 0 0}.$$

 The eigenvalues are the diagonal entries $1,\pi,0$. (The eigenvalue $1$ occurs twice, but it counts as one eigenvalue; in [diagonalization] we will define the notion of algebraic multiplicity of an eigenvalue.)

nodes.title: rational-root-thm
nodes.body: Suppose that $A$ is an $n\times n$ matrix whose characteristic polynomial $f(\lambda)$ has integer (whole-number) entries. Then all rational roots of its characteristic polynomial are integer divisors of $\det(A)$.

nodes.title: charpoly-eg-rat-root
nodes.body:
Find the eigenvalues of the matrix

$$A = \mat{7 0 3; -3 2 -3; -3 0 -1}.$$

 Hint: one eigenvalue is an integer.

 We compute the characteristic polynomial by expanding cofactors along the first row:

$$\begin{split}
 f(\lambda) = \det(A - \lambda I_3)
 \amp= \det\mat{7-\lambda, 0 3; -3 2-\lambda, -3; -3 0 -1-\lambda} \\
 \amp= (7-\lambda)(2-\lambda)(-1-\lambda) + 3\cdot 3(2-\lambda) \\
 \amp= -\lambda^3 + 8\lambda^2 - 14\lambda + 4.
 \end{split}$$

 The determinant of $A$ is the constant term $f(0) = 4$; its integer divisors are $\pm 1,\pm 2,\pm 4$. We check which are roots:

$$f(1) = -3 \quad f(-1) = 27 \quad f(2) = 0 \quad f(-2) = 72 \quad f(4) = 12 \quad f(-4) = 252.$$

 The only rational root of $f(\lambda)$ is $\lambda=2$. We divide by $\lambda-2$ using polynomial long division:

$$\frac{-\lambda^3 + 8\lambda^2 - 14\lambda + 4}{\lambda-2} = -\lambda^2 + 6\lambda - 2.$$

 We can use the quadratic formula to find the roots of the quotient:

$$\lambda = \frac{-6 \pm\sqrt{36 - 4\cdot 2}}{-2}
 = 3\pm\sqrt 7.$$

 We have factored $f$ completely:

$$f(\lambda) = -(\lambda-2)\bigl(\lambda-(3+\sqrt7)\bigr)\bigl(\lambda-(3-\sqrt7)\bigr).$$

 Therefore, the eigenvalues of $A$ are $2,\,3+\sqrt7,\,3-\sqrt7.$

nodes.title: charpoly-eg-0-eval
nodes.body:
Find the eigenvalues of the matrix

$$A = \mat{7 0 3; -3 2 -3; 4 2 0}.$$

 We compute the characteristic polynomial by expanding cofactors along the first row:

$$\begin{split}
 f(\lambda) = \det(A - \lambda I_3)
 \amp= \det\mat{7-\lambda, 0 3; -3 2-\lambda, -3; 4 2 -\lambda} \\
 \amp= (7-\lambda)\bigl(-\lambda(2-\lambda)+6\bigr) + 3\bigl(-6-4(2-\lambda)\bigr) \\
 \amp= -\lambda^3 + 9\lambda^2 - 8\lambda.
 \end{split}$$

 The constant term is zero, so $A$ has determinant zero. We factor out $\lambda$, then eyeball the roots of the quadratic factor:

$$f(\lambda) = -\lambda(\lambda^2-9\lambda+8) = -\lambda(\lambda-1)(\lambda-8).$$

 Therefore, the eigenvalues of $A$ are $0,1,$ and $8$.

nodes.title: Complex Eigenvalues
nodes.body:
Learn to find complex eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a matrix.

Learn to recognize a rotation-scaling matrix, and compute by how much the matrix rotates and scales.

Understand the geometry of $2\times 2$ and $3\times 3$ matrices with a complex eigenvalue.

Recipes: a $2\times 2$ matrix with a complex eigenvalue is similar to a rotation-scaling matrix, the eigenvector trick for $2\times 2$ matrices.

Pictures: the geometry of matrices with a complex eigenvalue.

Theorems: the rotation-scaling theorem, the block diagonalization theorem.

Vocabulary word: rotation-scaling matrix.

 In [diagonalization], we saw that an $n \times n$ matrix whose characteristic polynomial has $n$ distinct real roots is diagonalizable: it is similar to a diagonal matrix, which is much simpler to analyze. The other possibility is that a matrix has complex roots, and that is the focus of this section. It turns out that such a matrix is similar (in the $2\times 2$ case) to a rotation-scaling matrix, which is also relatively easy to understand.

 In a certain sense, this entire section is analogous to [diagonalization], with rotation-scaling matrices playing the role of diagonal matrices.

 In [diagonalization], we saw that a matrix whose characteristic polynomial has distinct real roots is diagonalizable: it is similar to a diagonal matrix, which is much simpler to analyze. In this section, we study matrices whose characteristic polynomial has complex roots. If a matrix has distinct complex eigenvalues, then it is also diagonalizable, but it similar to a diagonal matrix with complex entries. The geometric interpretation of such a matrix is a subtle question, which is treated in detail in the full version of the book.

 See [complex-numbers] for a review of the complex numbers.

nodes.title: Matrices with Complex Eigenvalues
nodes.body:
As a consequence of the [fund-thm-alg] as applied to the characteristic polynomial, we see that:

 We can compute a corresponding (complex) eigenvector in exactly the same way as before: by row reducing the matrix $A - \lambda I_n$. Now, however, we have to do arithmetic with complex numbers.

 If $A$ is a matrix with real entries, then its characteristic polynomial has real coefficients, so this [cplx-nums-root-pairs] implies that its complex eigenvalues come in conjugate pairs. In the first example, we notice that

$$\begin{split}
 1+i \text{ has an eigenvector }
 \amp v_1 = \vec{i 1} \\
 1-i \text{ has an eigenvector }
 \amp v_2 = \vec{-i 1}.
 \end{split}$$

 In the second example,

$$\begin{split}
 \frac{4+3i}5 \text{ has an eigenvector }
 \amp v_1 = \vec{-12-9i -9+12i 25} \\
 \frac{4-3i}5 \text{ has an eigenvector }
 \amp v_2 = \vec{-12+9i -9-12i 25}
 \end{split}$$

 In these cases, an eigenvector for the conjugate eigenvalue is simply the conjugate eigenvector (the eigenvector obtained by conjugating each entry of the first eigenvector). This is always true. Indeed, if $Av=\lambda v$ then 
$$A \bar v = \bar{Av} = \bar{\lambda v} = \bar \lambda \bar v,$$
 which exactly says that $\bar v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ with eigenvalue $\bar \lambda$.

 Since it can be tedious to divide by complex numbers while row reducing, it is useful to learn the following trick, which works equally well for matrices with real entries.

 Indeed, since $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue, we know that $A-\lambda I_2$ is not an invertible matrix. It follows that the rows are collinear (otherwise the determinant is nonzero), so that the second row is automatically a (complex) multiple of the first:

$$\mat{z w; \star, \star} = \mat{z w; cz cw}.$$

 It is obvious that ${-w\choose z}$ is in the null space of this matrix, as is ${w\choose -z}$, for that matter. Note that we never had to compute the second row of $A-\lambda I_2$, let alone row reduce!

 In this [cplx-evals-eg22-a] we found the eigenvectors ${i\choose 1}$ and ${-i\choose 1}$ for the eigenvalues $1+i$ and $1-i$, respectively, but in this [cplx-evals-eg22-b] we found the eigenvectors ${1\choose -i}$ and ${1\choose i}$ for the same eigenvalues of the same matrix. These vectors do not look like multiples of each other at firstbut since we now have complex numbers at our disposal, we can see that they actually are multiples:

$$-i\vec{i 1} = \vec{1 -i} \qquad i\vec{-i 1} = \vec{1 i}.$$

nodes.title: A 2\times 2 matrix
A 3\times 3 matrix
A 2\times 2 matrix, the easy way
nodes.body:
Find the complex eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the matrix

$$A = \mat{1 -1; 1 1}.$$

 Since the characteristic polynomial of a $2\times 2$ matrix $A$ is $f(\lambda) = \lambda^2-\Tr(A)\lambda + \det(A)$, its roots are

$$\lambda = \frac{\Tr(A)\pm\sqrt{\Tr(A)^2-4\det(A)}}2
 = \frac{2\pm\sqrt{4-8}}2 = 1\pm i.$$

 To find an eigenvector with eigenvalue $1+i$, we compute

$$A - (1+i)I_2 = \mat{-i -1; \star, \star}
 \;\xrightarrow{\text{eigenvector}}\; v_1 = \vec{1 -i}.$$

 The eigenvector for the conjugate eigenvalue is the complex conjugate:

$$v_2 = \bar v_1 = \vec{1 i}.$$

rotation-scaling matrix
nodes.body:
A rotation-scaling matrix is a $2\times 2$ matrix of the form

$$\mat{a -b; b a},$$

 where $a$ and $b$ are real numbers, not both equal to zero.

nodes.title: Proof: cplx-diagonalization-thm
nodes.body:
First we need to show that $\Re(v)$ and $\Im(v)$ are linearly independent, since otherwise $C$ is not invertible. If not, then there exist real numbers $x,y,$ not both equal to zero, such that $x\Re(v) + y\Im(v) = 0$. Then

$$\begin{split}
 (y+ix)v \amp= (y+ix)\bigl(\Re(v)+i\Im(v)\bigr) \\
 \amp= y\Re(v) - x\Im(v) + \left(x\Re(v) + y\Im(v)\right)i \\
 \amp= y\Re(v) - x\Im(v).
 \end{split}$$

 Now, $(y+ix)v$ is also an eigenvector of $A$ with eigenvalue $\lambda$, as it is a scalar multiple of $v$. But we just showed that $(y+ix)v$ is a vector with real entries, and any real eigenvector of a real matrix has a real eigenvalue. Therefore, $\Re(v)$ and $\Im(v)$ must be linearly independent after all.

 Let $\lambda = a+bi$ and $v = {x+yi\choose z+wi}$. We observe that

$$\begin{split}
 Av = \lambda v \amp= (a+bi)\vec{x+yi z+wi} \\
 \amp= \vec{(ax-by)+(ay+bx)i (az-bw)+(aw+bz)i} \\
 \amp= \vec{ax-by az-bw} + i\vec{ay+bx aw+bz}.
 \end{split}$$

 On the other hand, we have

$$A\left(\vec{x z} + i\vec{y w}\right)
 = A\vec{x z} + iA\vec{y w}
 = A\Re(v) + iA\Im(v).$$

 Matching real and imaginary parts gives

$$A\Re(v) = \vec{ax-by az-bw} \qquad
 A\Im(v) = \vec{ay+bx aw+bz}.$$

 Now we compute $CBC\inv\Re(v)$ and $CBC\inv\Im(v)$. Since $Ce_1 = \Re(v)$ and $Ce_2 = \Im(v)$, we have $C\inv\Re(v) = e_1$ and $C\inv\Im(v)=e_2$, so

$$\begin{split}
 CBC\inv\Re(v) \amp= CBe_1 = C\vec{a -b} = a\Re(v)-b\Im(v) \\
 \amp= a\vec{x z} - b\vec{y w}
 = \vec{ax-by az-bw} = A\Re(v) \\
 CBC\inv\Im(v) \amp= CBe_2 = C\vec{b a} = b\Re(v)+a\Im(v) \\
 \amp= b\vec{x z} + a\vec{y w}
 = \vec{ay+bx aw+bz} = A\Im(v).
 \end{split}$$

 Therefore, $A\Re(v) = CBC\inv\Re(v)$ and $A\Im(v) = CBC\inv\Im(v)$.

 Since $\Re(v)$ and $\Im(v)$ are linearly independent, they form a basis for $\R^2$. Let $w$ be any vector in $\R^2$, and write $w = c\Re(v) + d\Im(v)$. Then

$$\begin{split}
 Aw \amp= A\bigl(c\Re(v) + d\Im(v)\bigr) \\
 \amp= cA\Re(v) + dA\Im(v) \\
 \amp= cCBC\inv\Re(v) + dCBC\inv\Im(v) \\
 \amp= CBC\inv\bigl(c\Re(v) + d\Im(v)\bigr) \\
 \amp= CBC\inv w.
 \end{split}$$

 This proves that $A = CBC\inv$.

nodes.title: Classification of 2\times 2 matrices up to similarity
nodes.body:
At this point, we can write down the simplest possible matrix which is similar to any given $2\times 2$ matrix $A$. There are four cases:

 $A$ has two real eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\lambda_2$. In this case, $A$ is diagonalizable, so $A$ is similar to the matrix

$$\mat{\lambda_1 0; 0 \lambda_2}.$$

 This representation is unique up to reordering the eigenvalues.

 $A$ has one real eigenvalue $\lambda$ of geometric multiplicity $2$. In this case, we saw in this [diag-cases-22] that $A$ is equal to the matrix

$$\mat{\lambda, 0; 0 \lambda}.$$

 $A$ has one real eigenvalue $\lambda$ of geometric multiplicity $1$. In this case, $A$ is not diagonalizable, and we saw in this [diag-rem-all-nondiag] that $A$ is similar to the matrix

$$\mat{\lambda, 1; 0 \lambda}.$$

 $A$ has no real eigenvalues. In this case, $A$ has a complex eigenvalue $\lambda$, and $A$ is similar to the rotation-scaling matrix

$$\mat{\Re(\lambda) \Im(\lambda); -\Im(\lambda) \Re(\lambda)}$$

 by the [cplx-diagonalization-thm]. By this [cplx-eval-rot-scale], the eigenvalues of a rotation-scaling matrix $\smallmat a{-b}ba$ are $a\pm bi$, so that two rotation-scaling matrices $\smallmat a{-b}ba$ and $\smallmat c{-d}dc$ are similar if and only if $a=c$ and $b=\pm d$.
nodes.context: Geometry of 2\times 2 Matrices with a Complex Eigenvalue

nodes.title: Block Diagonalization
nodes.body:
For matrices larger than $2\times 2$, there is a theorem that combines the [diagonalization-thm] and the [cplx-diagonalization-thm]. It says essentially that a matrix is similar to a matrix with parts that look like a diagonal matrix, and parts that look like a rotation-scaling matrix.

 The [block-diag-thm] is proved in the same way as the [diagonalization-thm] and the [cplx-diagonalization-thm]. It is best understood in the case of $3\times 3$ matrices.

nodes.title: block diagonal
nodes.body:
Let $A$ be a real $n\times n$ matrix. Suppose that for each (real or complex) eigenvalue, the algebraic multiplicity equals the geometric multiplicity. Then $A = CBC\inv$, where $B$ and $C$ are as follows:

 The matrix $B$ is block diagonal, where the blocks are $1\times 1$ blocks containing the real eigenvalues (with their multiplicities), or $2\times 2$ blocks containing the matrices

$$\mat{\Re(\lambda) \Im(\lambda); -\Im(\lambda) \Re(\lambda)}$$

 for each non-real eigenvalue $\lambda$ (with multiplicity).

 The columns of $C$ form bases for the eigenspaces for the real eigenvectors, or come in pairs $\bigl(\,\Re(v)\;\Im(v)\,\bigr)$ for the non-real eigenvectors.

imaginary number
nodes.body:
\CThe complex numbers

 The imaginary number $i$ is defined to satisfy the equation $i^2 = -1$.

 A complex number is a number of the form $a+bi$, where $a,b$ are real numbers.

 The set of all complex numbers is denoted $\C$.

nodes.title: fund-thm-alg
nodes.body:
Every polynomial of degree $n$ has exactly $n$ (real and) complex roots, counted with multiplicity.

 Equivalently, if $f(x) = x^n + a_{n-1}x^{n-1} + \cdots + a_1x + a_0$ is a polynomial of degree $n$, then $f$ factors as

$$f(x) = (x-\lambda_1)(x-\lambda_2)\cdots(x-\lambda_n)$$

 for (not necessarily distinct) complex numbers $\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\ldots,\lambda_n$.

nodes.title: Cofactor Expansions
nodes.body:
Learn to recognize which methods are best suited to compute the determinant of a given matrix.

Recipes: the determinant of a $3\times 3$ matrix, compute the determinant using cofactor expansions.

Vocabulary words: minor, cofactor.

 In this section, we give a recursive formula for the determinant of a matrix, called a cofactor expansion. The formula is recursive in that we will compute the determinant of an $n\times n$ matrix assuming we already know how to compute the determinant of an $(n-1)\times(n-1)$ matrix.

 At the end is a supplementary subsection on Cramers rule and a cofactor formula for the inverse of a matrix.

nodes.title: Cofactor Expansions
nodes.body:
A recursive formula must have a starting point. For cofactor expansions, the starting point is the case of $1\times 1$ matrices. The definition of determinant directly implies that

$$\det\mat a=a.$$

 To describe cofactor expansions, we need to introduce some notation.

 Note that the signs of the cofactors follow a checkerboard pattern. Namely, $(-1)^{i+j}$ is pictured in this matrix:

$$\def\a{\textcolor{seq-green}{+}} \def\b{\textcolor{seq-blue}{-}}
 \mat{\a,\b,\a,\b ; \b,\a,\b,\a ; \a,\b,\a,\b; \b,\a,\b,\a}.$$

 The cofactors $C_{ij}$ of an $n\times n$ matrix are determinants of $(n-1)\times(n-1)$ submatrices. Hence the following theorem is in fact a recursive procedure for computing the determinant.

 Note that the theorem actually gives $2n$ different formulas for the determinant: one for each row and one for each column. For instance, the formula for cofactor expansion along the first column is

$$\begin{split}
 \det(A) = \sum_{i=1}^n a_{i1}C_{i1}
 \amp= a_{11}C_{11} + a_{21}C_{21} + \cdots + a_{n1}C_{n1} \\
 \amp= a_{11}\det(A_{11}) - a_{21}\det(A_{21}) + a_{31}\det(A_{31}) - \cdots \pm a_{n1}\det(A_{n1}).
 \end{split}$$

 Remember, the determinant of a matrix is just a number, defined by the four [det-defn-the-defn], so to be clear:

 Now that we have a recursive formula for the determinant, we can finally prove the [det-defn-unique].

 The formula for the determinant of a $3\times 3$ matrix looks too complicated to memorize outright. Fortunately, there is the following mnemonic device.

 Alternatively, it is not necessary to repeat the first two columns if you allow your diagonals to wrap around the sides of a matrix, like in Pac-Man or Asteroids.

 Cofactor expansions are most useful when computing the determinant of a matrix that has a row or column with several zero entries. Indeed, if the $(i,j)$ entry of $A$ is zero, then there is no reason to compute the $(i,j)$ cofactor. In the following example we compute the determinant of a matrix with two zeros in the fourth column by expanding cofactors along the fourth column.

 Cofactor expansions are also very useful when computing the determinant of a matrix with unknown entries. Indeed, it is inconvenient to row reduce in this case, because one cannot be sure whether an entry containing an unknown is a pivot or not.

 It is often most efficient to use a combination of several techniques when computing the determinant of a matrix. Indeed, when expanding cofactors on a matrix, one can compute the determinants of the cofactors in whatever way is most convenient. Or, one can perform row and column operations to clear some entries of a matrix before expanding cofactors, as in the previous example.

nodes.title: minor,
nodes.body:
A_{ij}Minor of a matrix
 C_{ij}Cofactor of a matrix

Let $A$ be an $n\times n$ matrix.

 The $(i,j)$ minor, denoted $A_{ij}$, is the $(n-1)\times (n-1)$ matrix obtained from $A$ by deleting the $i$th row and the $j$th column.

 The $(i,j)$ cofactor $C_{ij}$ is defined in terms of the minor by

$$C_{ij}=(-1)^{i+j}\det(A_{ij}).$$

nodes.title: determinant-cofactors-example-1
Cofactor expansion
nodes.body:
Let $A$ be an $n\times n$ matrix with entries $a_{ij}$.

 For any $i = 1,2,\ldots,n$, we have

$$\det(A) = \sum_{j=1}^n a_{ij}C_{ij}
 = a_{i1}C_{i1} + a_{i2}C_{i2} + \cdots + a_{in}C_{in}.$$

 This is called cofactor expansion along the $i$th row.

 For any $j = 1,2,\ldots,n$, we have

$$\det(A) = \sum_{i=1}^n a_{ij}C_{ij}
 = a_{1j}C_{1j} + a_{2j}C_{2j} + \cdots + a_{nj}C_{nj}.$$

 This is called cofactor expansion along the $j$th column.

nodes.title: Proof: Cofactor expansion
Proof: Cofactor Expansions
nodes.body:
Let us review what we actually proved in [determinants-definitions-properties]. We showed that if $\det\colon\{n\times n\text{ matrices}\}\to\R$ is any function satisfying the four [det-defn-the-defn] (or the three [det-defn-use-multi]), then it also satisfies all of the wonderful properties proved in that section. In particular, since $\det$ can be computed using row reduction by this [det-defn-ref-compute], it is uniquely characterized by the defining properties. What we did not prove was the existence of such a function, since we did not know that two different row reduction procedures would always compute the same answer.

 Consider the function $d$ defined by cofactor expansion along the first row:

$$d(A) = \sum_{i=1}^n (-1)^{i+1} a_{i1}\det(A_{i1}).$$

 If we assume that the determinant exists for $(n-1)\times(n-1)$ matrices, then there is no question that the function $d$ exists, since we gave a formula for it. Moreover, we showed in the proof of the [det-cofact-expansion] above that $d$ satisfies the three alternative defining properties of the determinant, again only assuming that the determinant exists for $(n-1)\times(n-1)$ matrices. This proves the existence of the determinant for $n\times n$ matrices!

 This is an example of a proof by mathematical induction. We start by noticing that $\det\mat a = a$ satisfies the four defining properties of the determinant of a $1\times 1$ matrix. Then we showed that the determinant of $n\times n$ matrices exists, assuming the determinant of $(n-1)\times(n-1)$ matrices exists. This implies that all determinants exist, by the following chain of logic:

$$1\times 1\text{ exists} \;\implies\;
 2\times 2\text{ exists} \;\implies\;
 3\times 3\text{ exists} \;\implies\; \cdots.$$

nodes.title: determinant-cofactors-example-2
determinant-cofactors-example-3
determinant-cofactors-example-4
determinant-cofactors-example-5
nodes.body:
Compute the determinant of this matrix containing the unknown $\lambda$:

$$A = \mat{-\lambda, 2 7 12; 3 1-\lambda, 2 -4; 0 1 -\lambda, 7; 0 0 0 2-\lambda}.$$

 First we expand cofactors along the fourth row:

$$\begin{split}
 \det(A) \amp= 0\det\mat\cdots + 0\det\mat\cdots + 0\det\mat\cdots \\
 \amp\qquad+
 (2-\lambda)\det\mat{-\lambda, 2 7; 3 1-\lambda, 2; 0 1 -\lambda}.
 \end{split}$$

 We only have to compute one cofactor. To do so, first we clear the $(3,3)$-entry by performing the column replacement $C_3 = C_3 + \lambda C_2$, which does not change the determinant:

$$\det\mat{-\lambda, 2 7; 3 1-\lambda, 2; 0 1 -\lambda}
 = \det\mat{-\lambda, 2 7+2\lambda; 3 1-\lambda, 2+\lambda(1-\lambda); 0 1 0}.$$

 Now we expand cofactors along the third row to find

$$\begin{split}
 \det\mat{-\lambda, 2 7+2\lambda; 3 1-\lambda, 2+\lambda(1-\lambda); 0 1 0}
 \amp= (-1)^{2+3}\det\mat{-\lambda, 7+2\lambda; 3 2+\lambda(1-\lambda)} \\
 \amp= -\biggl(-\lambda\bigl(2+\lambda(1-\lambda)\bigr) - 3(7+2\lambda) \biggr) \\
 \amp= -\lambda^3 + \lambda^2 + 8\lambda + 21.
 \end{split}$$

 Therefore, we have

$$\det(A) = (2-\lambda)(-\lambda^3 + \lambda^2 + 8\lambda + 21)
 = \lambda^4 - 3\lambda^3 - 6\lambda^2 - 5\lambda + 42.$$

nodes.title: Cramers Rule and Matrix Inverses
nodes.body:
Recall from this [matrix-inv-22] that one can compute the determinant of a $2\times 2$ matrix using the rule

$$A = \mat{d -b; -c a} \quad\implies\quad
 A\inv = \frac 1{\det(A)}\mat{d -b; -c a}.$$

 We computed the cofactors of a $2\times 2$ matrix in this [det-cofactor-22]; using $C_{11}=d,\,C_{12}=-c,\,C_{21}=-b,\,C_{22}=a$, we can rewrite the above formula as

$$A\inv = \frac 1{\det(A)}\mat{C_{11} C_{21}; C_{12} C_{22}}.$$

 It turns out that this formula generalizes to $n\times n$ matrices.

 \adj(A)Adjugate matrix
 The matrix of cofactors is sometimes called the adjugate matrix of $A$, and is denoted $\adj(A)$:

$$\adj(A) = \mat{C_{11} C_{21} \cdots, C_{n-1,1} C_{n1};
 C_{12} C_{22} \cdots, C_{n-1,2} C_{n2};
 \vdots, \vdots, \ddots, \vdots, \vdots;
 C_{1,n-1} C_{2,n-1} \cdots, C_{n-1,n-1} C_{n,n-1};
 C_{1n} C_{2n} \cdots, C_{n-1,n} C_{nn}}.$$

 Note that the $(i,j)$ cofactor $C_{ij}$ goes in the $(j,i)$ entry the adjugate matrix, not the $(i,j)$ entry: the adjugate matrix is the transpose of the cofactor matrix.

 It is clear from the previous example that [det-cofact-inv-cramer-fn] is a very inefficient way of computing the inverse of a matrix, compared to augmenting by the identity matrix and row reducing, as in this [matrix-inv-computing]. However, it has its uses.

 If a matrix has unknown entries, then it is difficult to compute its inverse using row reduction, for the same reason it is difficult to compute the determinant that way: one cannot be sure whether an entry containing an unknown is a pivot or not.

 This formula is useful for theoretical purposes. Notice that the only denominators in [det-cofact-inv-cramer-fn] occur when dividing by the determinant: computing cofactors only involves multiplication and addition, never division. This means, for instance, that if the determinant is very small, then any measurement error in the entries of the matrix is greatly magnified when computing the inverse. In this way, [det-cofact-inv-cramer-fn] is useful in error analysis.

 The proof of the [det-cofact-inv-cramer] uses an interesting trick called Cramers Rule, which gives a formula for the entries of the solution of an invertible matrix equation.

 Now we use Cramers rule to prove the first [det-cofact-inv-cramer] of this subsection.

nodes.title: det-cofact-inv-cramer
determinant-cofactors-remark-1
nodes.body:
In fact, one always has
 $A\cdot\adj(A) = \adj(A)\cdot A = \det(A)I_n,$
 whether or not $A$ is invertible.

nodes.title: determinant-cofactors-example-6
nodes.body:
Use the [det-cofact-inv-cramer] to compute $A\inv$, where

$$A = \mat{1 0 1; 0 1 1; 1 1 0}.$$

 The minors are:

\begin{align*}
 A_{11} \amp= \mat{1 1; 1 0} \amp
 A_{12} \amp= \mat{0 1; 1 0} \amp
 A_{13} \amp= \mat{0 1; 1 1} \\
 A_{21} \amp= \mat{0 1; 1 0} \amp
 A_{22} \amp= \mat{1 1; 1 0} \amp
 A_{23} \amp= \mat{1 0; 1 1} \\
 A_{31} \amp= \mat{0 1; 1 1} \amp
 A_{32} \amp= \mat{1 1; 0 1} \amp
 A_{33} \amp= \mat{1 0; 0 1}
\end{align*}

 The cofactors are:

\begin{align*}
 C_{11} \amp= -1 \amp C_{12} \amp= \phantom-1 \amp C_{13} \amp= -1 \\
 C_{21} \amp= \phantom-1 \amp C_{22} \amp= -1 \amp C_{23} \amp= -1 \\
 C_{31} \amp= -1 \amp C_{32} \amp= -1 \amp C_{33} \amp= \phantom-1
\end{align*}

 Expanding along the first row, we compute the determinant to be

$$\det(A) = 1\cdot C_{11} + 0\cdot C_{12} + 1\cdot C_{13} = -2.$$

 Therefore, the inverse is

$$A\inv = \frac 1{\det(A)}
 \mat{C_{11} C_{21} C_{31}; C_{12} C_{22} C_{32}; C_{13} C_{23} C_{33}}
= -\frac12\mat[r]{-1 1 -1; 1 -1 -1; -1 -1 1}.$$

nodes.title: Cramers Rule
nodes.body:
Let $x = (x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)$ be the solution of $Ax=b$, where $A$ is an invertible $n\times n$ matrix and $b$ is a vector in $\R^n$. Let $A_i$ be the matrix obtained from $A$ by replacing the $i$th column by $b$. Then

$$x_i = \frac{\det(A_i)}{\det(A)}.$$

nodes.title: Proof: Cramers Rule
determinant-cofactors-example-7
nodes.body:
Compute the solution of $Ax=b$ using Cramers rule, where

$$A = \mat{a b; c d} \qquad b = \vec{1 2}.$$

 Here the coefficients of $A$ are unknown, but $A$ may be assumed invertible.

 First we compute the determinants of the matrices obtained by replacing the columns of $A$ with $b$:

$$\begin{aligned}
 A_1 \amp= \mat{1 b; 2 d} \amp \det(A_1) \amp= d-2b
 \\ 
 A_2 \amp= \mat{a 1; c 2} \amp \det(A_2) \amp= 2a-c.
 \end{aligned}$$

 Now we compute

$$\frac{\det(A_1)}{\det(A)} = \frac{d-2b}{ad-bc}
 \qquad
 \frac{\det(A_2)}{\det(A)} = \frac{2a-c}{ad-bc}.$$

 It follows that

$$x = \frac 1{ad-bc}\vec{d-2b 2a-c}.$$
