nodes.title: dimension-basis-nulspace
nodes.body: The vectors attached to the free variables in the parametric vector form of the solution set of $Ax=0$ form a basis of $\Nul(A)$.
nodes.context: Computing a Basis for a Subspace

nodes.title: A basis of a subspace
nodes.body:
Let $V$ be the subspace defined by

$$V = \left\{\vec{x y z}\bigm| x + 2y = z\right\}.$$

 Find a basis for $V$. What is $\dim(V)$?

 First we notice that $V$ is exactly the solution set of the homogeneous linear equation $x + 2y - z = 0$. Hence $V = \Nul\mat{1 2 -1}.$ This matrix is in reduced row echelon form; the parametric form of the general solution is $x = -2y + z$, so the parametric vector form is

$$\vec{x y z} = y\vec{-2 1 0} + z\vec{1 0 1}.$$

 It follows that a basis is

$$\left\{\vec{-2 1 0},\;\vec{1 0 1}\right\}.$$

 Since $V$ has a basis with two vectors, its dimension is $2$: it is a plane.
nodes.context: Computing a Basis for a Subspace

nodes.title: The Basis Theorem
nodes.body:
Recall that $\{v_1,v_2,\ldots,v_n\}$ forms a basis for $\R^n$ if and only if the matrix $A$ with columns $v_1,v_2,\ldots,v_n$ has a pivot in every row and column (see this [dimension-eg-Rn-any]). Since $A$ is an $n\times n$ matrix, these two conditions are equivalent: the vectors span if and only if they are linearly independent.
 The basis theorem is an abstract version of the preceding statement, that applies to any subspace.

 In other words, if you already know that $\dim V = m$, and if you have a set of $m$ vectors $\cB = \{v_1,v_2,\ldots,v_m\}$ in $V$, then you only have to check one of:

$\cB$ is linearly independent, or

$\cB$ spans $V$,

 in order for $\cB$ to be a basis of $V$. If you did not already know that $\dim V = m$, then you would have to check both properties.

 To put it yet another way, suppose we have a set of vectors $\cB = \{v_1,v_2,\ldots,v_m\}$ in a subspace $V$. Then if any two of the following statements is true, the third must also be true:

$\cB$ is linearly independent,

$\cB$ spans $V$, and

$\dim V = m.$

For example, if $V$ is a plane, then any two noncollinear vectors in $V$ form a basis.

nodes.title: basis-theorem
nodes.body:
Let $V$ be a subspace of dimension $m$. Then:

Any $m$ linearly independent vectors in $V$ form a basis for $V$.

Any $m$ vectors that span $V$ form a basis for $V$.

nodes.title: Proof: basis-theorem
nodes.body:
Suppose that $\cB = \{v_1,v_2,\ldots,v_m\}$ is a set of linearly independent vectors in $V$. In order to show that $\cB$ is a basis for $V$, we must prove that $V = \Span\{v_1,v_2,\ldots,v_m\}.$ If not, then there exists some vector $v_{m+1}$ in $V$ that is not contained in $\Span\{v_1,v_2,\ldots,v_m\}.$ By the [linindep-increasing-span], the set $\{v_1,v_2,\ldots,v_m,v_{m+1}\}$ is also linearly independent. Continuing in this way, we keep choosing vectors until we eventually do have a linearly independent spanning set: say $V = \Span\{v_1,v_2,\ldots,v_m,\ldots,v_{m+k}\}$. Then $\{v_1,v_2,\ldots,v_{m+k}\}$ is a basis for $V$, which implies that $\dim(V) = m+k > m$. But we were assuming that $V$ has dimension $m$, so $\cB$ must have already been a basis.

 Now suppose that $\cB = \{v_1,v_2,\ldots,v_m\}$ spans $V$. If $\cB$ is not linearly independent, then by this [linindep-criterion-inspan], we can remove some number of vectors from $\cB$ without shrinking its span. After reordering, we can assume that we removed the last $k$ vectors without shrinking the span, and that we cannot remove any more. Now $V = \Span\{v_1,v_2,\ldots,v_{m-k}\}$, and $\{v_1,v_2,\ldots,v_{m-k}\}$ is a basis for $V$ because it is linearly independent. This implies that $\dim V=m-k < m$. But we were assuming that $\dim V = m$, so $\cB$ must have already been a basis.

nodes.title: Two noncollinear vectors form a basis of a plane
nodes.body:
Find a basis of the subspace

$$V = \Span\left\{\vec{1 -2 2},\;\vec{2 -3 4},\;\vec{0 4 0},\;\vec{-1 5 -2}\right\}$$

 which is different from the bases in this [dimension-eg-basis-span] and this [dimension-eg-basis-span2].

 We know from the previous examples that $\dim V = 2$. By the [basis-theorem], it suffices to find any two noncollinear vectors in $V$. We write two linear combinations of the four given spanning vectors, chosen at random:

$$w_1 = \vec{1 -2 2} + \vec{2 -3 4} = \vec{3 -5 6} \qquad
 w_2 = -\vec{2 -3 4} + \frac 12\vec{0 4 0} = \vec{-2 5 -4}.$$

 Since $w_1,w_2$ are not collinear, $\cB = \{w_1,w_2\}$ is a basis for $V$.

 A picture of the plane $V$ and its basis $\cB = \{w_1,w_2\}$.

nodes.title: Finding a basis by inspection
nodes.body:
Find a basis for the plane

$$V = \left\{\vec{x_1 x_2 x_3}\bigm| x_1 + x_2 = x_3\right\}$$

 by inspection. (This plane is expressed in [set-builder-notation].)

 First note that $V$ is the null space of the matrix $\mat{1 1 -1}$; this matrix is in reduced row echelon form and has two free variables, so $V$ is indeed a plane. We write down two vectors satisfying $x_1 + x_2 = x_3$:

$$v_1 = \vec{1 0 1} \qquad v_2 = \vec{0 1 1}.$$

 Since $v_1$ and $v_2$ are not collinear, they are linearly independent; since $\dim(V) = 2$, the basis theorem implies that $\{v_1,v_2\}$ is a basis for $V$.

nodes.title: Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors
nodes.body:
Learn the definition of eigenvector and eigenvalue.

Learn to find eigenvectors and eigenvalues geometrically.

Learn to decide if a number is an eigenvalue of a matrix, and if so, how to find an associated eigenvector.

Recipe: find a basis for the $\lambda$-eigenspace.

Pictures: whether or not a vector is an eigenvector, eigenvectors of standard matrix transformations.

Theorem: the expanded invertible matrix theorem.

Vocabulary word: eigenspace.

Essential vocabulary words: eigenvector, eigenvalue.

 In this section, we define eigenvalues and eigenvectors. These form the most important facet of the structure theory of square matrices. As such, eigenvalues and eigenvectors tend to play a key role in the real-life applications of linear algebra.

nodes.title: Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors
Verifying eigenvectors
Verifying eigenvectors
nodes.body:
Consider the matrix

$$A = \mat{0 6 8; \frac 12 0 0; 0 \frac 12 0}
 \sptxt{and vectors} v = \vec{16 4 1} \qquad w = \vec{2 2 2}.$$

 Which are eigenvectors? What are their eigenvalues?

 We have

$$Av = \mat{0 6 8; \frac 12 0 0; 0 \frac 12 0}\vec{16 4 1}
 = \vec{32 8 2} = 2v.$$

 Hence, $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$, with eigenvalue $\lambda = 2$. On the other hand,

$$Aw = \mat{0 6 8; \frac 12 0 0; 0 \frac 12 0}\vec{2 2 2}
 = \vec{28 1 1},$$

 which is not a scalar multiple of $w$. Hence, $w$ is not an eigenvector of $A$.

nodes.title: An eigenvector with eigenvalue 0
nodes.body:
Let

$$A = \mat{1 3; 2 6} \qquad v = \vec{-3 1}.$$

 Is $v$ an eigenvector of $A$? If so, what is its eigenvalue?

 The product is

$$Av = \mat{1 3; 2 6}\vec{-3 1} = \vec{0 0} = 0v.$$

 Hence, $v$ is an eigenvector with eigenvalue zero.

 As noted above, an eigenvalue is allowed to be zero, but an eigenvector is not.

nodes.title: Projection
Identity
nodes.body:
Find all eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the identity matrix $I_n$.

 The identity matrix has the property that $I_nv = v$ for all vectors $v$ in $\R^n$. We can write this as $I_n v = 1\cdot v$, so every nonzero vector is an eigenvector with eigenvalue $1$.

 Every nonzero vector is an eigenvector of the identity matrix.

nodes.title: Dilation
Shear
Rotation
Eigenvectors with distinct eigenvalues are linearly independent
nodes.body: Let $v_1,v_2,\ldots,v_k$ be eigenvectors of a matrix $A$, and suppose that the corresponding eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\ldots,\lambda_k$ are distinct (all different from each other). Then $\{v_1,v_2,\ldots,v_k\}$ is linearly independent.

nodes.title: Proof: Eigenvectors with distinct eigenvalues are linearly independent
nodes.body:
Suppose that $\{v_1,v_2,\ldots,v_k\}$ were linearly dependent. According to the [linindep-increasing-span], this means that for some $j$, the vector $v_j$ is in $\Span\{v_1,v_2,\ldots,v_{j-1}\}.$ If we choose the first such $j$, then $\{v_1,v_2,\ldots,v_{j-1}\}$ is linearly independent. Note that $j > 1$ since $v_1\neq 0$.

 Since $v_j$ is in $\Span\{v_1,v_2,\ldots,v_{j-1}\},$, we can write

$$v_j = c_1v_1 + c_2v_2 + \cdots + c_{j-1}v_{j-1}$$

 for some scalars $c_1,c_2,\ldots,c_{j-1}$. Multiplying both sides of the above equation by $A$ gives

$$\begin{split}
 \lambda_jv_j =
 Av_j \amp= A\bigl(c_1v_1 + c_2v_2 + \cdots + c_{j-1}v_{j-1}\bigr) \\
 \amp= c_1Av_1 + c_2Av_2 + \cdots + c_{j-1}Av_{j-1} \\
 \amp= c_1\lambda_1v_1 + c_2\lambda_2v_2 + \cdots + c_{j-1}\lambda_{j-1}v_{j-1}.
 \end{split}$$

 Subtracting $\lambda_j$ times the first equation from the second gives

$$0 = \lambda_jv_j - \lambda_jv_j
 = c_1(\lambda_1-\lambda_j)v_1 + c_2(\lambda_2-\lambda_j)v_2 + \cdots + c_{j-1}(\lambda_{j-1}-\lambda_j)v_{j-1}.$$

 Since $\lambda_i\neq\lambda_j$ for $i \lt j$, this is an equation of linear dependence among $v_1,v_2,\ldots,v_{j-1}$, which is impossible because those vectors are linearly independent. Therefore, $\{v_1,v_2,\ldots,v_k\}$ must have been linearly independent after all.

nodes.title: Eigenspaces
nodes.body:
Suppose that $A$ is a square matrix. We already know how to check if a given vector is an eigenvector of $A$ and in that case to find the eigenvalue. Our next goal is to check if a given real number is an eigenvalue of $A$ and in that case to find all of the corresponding eigenvectors. Again this will be straightforward, but more involved. The only missing piece, then, will be to find the eigenvalues of $A$; this is the main content of [characteristic-polynomial].

 Let $A$ be an $n\times n$ matrix, and let $\lambda$ be a scalar. The eigenvectors with eigenvalue $\lambda$, if any, are the nonzero solutions of the equation $Av=\lambda v$. We can rewrite this equation as follows:

$$\begin{split}
 \amp Av = \lambda v \\
 \iff\quad \amp Av - \lambda v = 0 \\
 \iff\quad \amp Av - \lambda I_nv = 0 \\
 \iff\quad \amp(A - \lambda I_n)v = 0.
 \end{split}$$

 Therefore, the eigenvectors of $A$ with eigenvalue $\lambda$, if any, are the nontrivial solutions of the matrix equation $(A-\lambda I_n)v = 0$, i.e., the nonzero vectors in $\Nul(A-\lambda I_n)$. If this equation has no nontrivial solutions, then $\lambda$ is not an eigenvector of $A$.

 The above observation is important because it says that finding the eigenvectors for a given eigenvalue means solving a homogeneous system of equations. For instance, if

$$A = \mat{7 1 3; -3 2 -3; -3 -2 -1},$$

 then an eigenvector with eigenvalue $\lambda$ is a nontrivial solution of the matrix equation

$$\mat{7 1 3; -3 2 -3; -3 -2 -1}\vec{x y z} = \lambda \vec{x y z}.$$

 This translates to the system of equations

$$\syseq{
 7x + y + 3z = \lambda x ;
 -3x + 2y - 3z = \lambda y ;
 -3x - 2y - z = \lambda z
 }
 \quad\xrightarrow{\phantom{MMM}}\quad
 \syseq{
 (7-\lambda)x + y + 3z = 0 ;
 -3x + (2-\lambda)y - 3z = 0 ;
 -3x - 2y + (-1-\lambda)z = 0\rlap.
 }$$

 This is the same as the homogeneous matrix equation

$$\mat{7-\lambda, 1 3; -3 2-\lambda, -3; -3 -2 -1-\lambda}\vec{x y z} = 0,$$

 i.e., $(A-\lambda I_3)v = 0$.

 The $\lambda$-eigenspace is a subspace because it is the null space of a matrix, namely, the matrix $A-\lambda I_n$. This subspace consists of the zero vector and all eigenvectors of $A$ with eigenvalue $\lambda$.

 We conclude with an observation about the $0$-eigenspace of a matrix.

 Concretely, an eigenvector with eigenvalue $0$ is a nonzero vector $v$ such that $Av=0v$, i.e., such that $Av = 0$. These are exactly the nonzero vectors in the null space of $A$.

nodes.title: \lambda-eigenspace
nodes.body: Let $A$ be an $n\times n$ matrix, and let $\lambda$ be an eigenvalue of $A$. The $\lambda$-eigenspace of $A$ is the solution set of $(A-\lambda I_n)v=0$, i.e., the subspace $\Nul(A-\lambda I_n)$.

nodes.title: Computing eigenspaces
nodes.body:
For each of the numbers $\lambda = -2, 1, 3$, decide if $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of the matrix

$$A = \mat{2 -4; -1 -1},$$

 and if so, compute a basis for the $\lambda$-eigenspace.

 The number $3$ is an eigenvalue of $A$ if and only if $\Nul(A-3I_2)$ is nonzero. Hence, we have to solve the matrix equation $(A-3I_2)v = 0$. We have

$$A - 3I_2 = \mat{2 -4; -1 -1} - 3\mat{1 0; 0 1} = \mat{-1 -4; -1 -4}.$$

 The reduced row echelon form of this matrix is

$$\mat{1 4; 0 0}
 \quad\xrightarrow[\text{form}]{\text{parametric}}\quad
 \syseq{x = -4y; y = y}
 \quad\xrightarrow[\text{vector form}]{\text{parametric}}\quad
 \vec{x y} = y\vec{-4 1}.$$

 Since $y$ is a free variable, the null space of $A-3I_2$ is nonzero, so $3$ is an eigenvector. A basis for the $3$-eigenspace is $\bigl\{{-4\choose 1}\bigr\}.$

 Concretely, we have shown that the eigenvectors of $A$ with eigenvalue $3$ are exactly the nonzero multiples of ${-4\choose 1}$. In particular, $-4\choose 1$ is an eigenvector, which we can verify:

$$\mat{2 -4; -1 -1}\vec{-4 1} = \vec{-12 3} = 3\vec{-4 1}.$$

 The number $1$ is an eigenvalue of $A$ if and only if $\Nul(A-I_2)$ is nonzero. Hence, we have to solve the matrix equation $(A-I_2)v = 0$. We have

$$A - I_2 = \mat{2 -4; -1 -1} - \mat{1 0; 0 1} = \mat{1 -4; -1 -2}.$$

 This matrix has determinant $-6$, so it is invertible. By the [imt-1], we have $\Nul(A-I_2) = \{0\}$, so $1$ is not an eigenvalue.

 The eigenvectors of $A$ with eigenvalue $-2$, if any, are the nonzero solutions of the matrix equation $(A+2I_2)v = 0$. We have

$$A + 2I_2 = \mat{2 -4; -1 -1} + 2\mat{1 0; 0 1} = \mat{4 -4; -1 1}.$$

 The reduced row echelon form of this matrix is

$$\mat{1 -1; 0 0}
 \quad\xrightarrow[\text{form}]{\text{parametric}}\quad
 \syseq{x = y; y = y}
 \quad\xrightarrow[\text{vector form}]{\text{parametric}}\quad
 \vec{x y} = y\vec{1 1}.$$

 Hence there exist eigenvectors with eigenvalue $-2$, namely, any nonzero multiple of ${1\choose 1}.$ A basis for the $-2$-eigenspace is $\bigl\{{1\choose 1}\bigr\}.$

 The $3$-eigenspace is the line spanned by ${-4\choose 1}.$ This means that $A$ scales every vector in that line by a factor of $3$. Likewise, the $-2$-eigenspace is the line spanned by ${1\choose 1}.$ Click and drag the vector $x$ around to see how $A$ acts on that vector.

nodes.title: Computing eigenspaces
nodes.body:
For each of the numbers $\lambda=0, \frac 12, 2$, decide if $\lambda$ is an eigenvector of the matrix

$$A = \mat{7/2 0 3; -3/2 2 -3; -3/2 0 -1},$$

 and if so, compute a basis for the $\lambda$-eigenspace.

 The number $2$ is an eigenvalue of $A$ if and only if $\Nul(A-2I_3)$ is nonzero. Hence, we have to solve the matrix equation $(A-2I_3)v = 0$. We have

$$A - 2I_3 = \mat{7/2 0 3; -3/2 2 -3; -3/2 0 1} - 2\mat{1 0 0; 0 1 0; 0 0 1}
 = \mat{3/2 0 3; -3/2 0 -3; -3/2 0 -3}.$$

 The reduced row echelon form of this matrix is

$$\mat{1 0 2; 0 0 0; 0 0 0}
 \quad\xrightarrow[\text{form}]{\text{parametric}}\quad
 \syseq{x = -2z; y = y; z = z}
 \quad\xrightarrow[\text{vector form}]{\text{parametric}}\quad
 \vec{x y z} = y\vec{0 1 0} + z\vec{-2 0 1}.$$

 The matrix $A-2I_3$ has two free variables, so the null space of $A-2I_3$ is nonzero, and thus $2$ is an eigenvector. A basis for the $2$-eigenspace is

$$\left\{\vec{0 1 0},\,\vec{-2 0 1}\right\}.$$

 This is a plane in $\R^3$.

 The eigenvectors of $A$ with eigenvalue $\frac 12$, if any, are the nonzero solutions of the matrix equation $(A-\frac 12I_3)v = 0$. We have

$$A - \frac 12I_3 = \mat{7/2 0 3; -3/2 2 -3; -3/2 0 1} - \frac 12\mat{1 0 0; 0 1 0; 0 0 1}
 = \mat{3 0 3; -3/2 3/2 -3; -3/2 0 -3/2}.$$

 The reduced row echelon form of this matrix is

$$\mat{1 0 1; 0 1 -1; 0 0 0}
 \quad\xrightarrow[\text{form}]{\text{parametric}}\quad
 \syseq{x = -z; y = z; z = z}
 \quad\xrightarrow[\text{vector form}]{\text{parametric}}\quad
 \vec{x y z} = z\vec{-1 1 1}.$$

 Hence there exist eigenvectors with eigenvalue $\frac 12$, so $\frac 12$ is an eigenvalue. A basis for the $\frac 12$-eigenspace is

$$\left\{\vec{-1 1 1}\right\}.$$

 This is a line in $\R^3$.

 The number $0$ is an eigenvalue of $A$ if and only if $\Nul(A-0I_3) = \Nul(A)$ is nonzero. This is the same as asking whether $A$ is noninvertible, by the [imt-1]. The determinant of $A$ is $\det(A) = 2\neq 0$, so $A$ is invertible by the [det-defn-invert-prop]. It follows that $0$ is not an eigenvalue of $A$.

 The $2$-eigenspace is the violet plane. This means that $A$ scales every vector in that plane by a factor of $2$. The $\frac 12$-eigenspace is the green line. Click and drag the vector $x$ around to see how $A$ acts on that vector.

nodes.title: Reflection
nodes.body:
Let $T\colon\R^2\to\R^2$ be the linear transformation that reflects over the line $L$ defined by $y=-x$, and let $A$ be the matrix for $T$. Find all eigenspaces of $A$.

 We showed in this [evec-eg-reflection] that all eigenvectors with eigenvalue $1$ lie on $L$, and all eigenvectors with eigenvalue $-1$ lie on the line $L^\perp$ that is perpendicular to $L$. Hence, $L$ is the $1$-eigenspace, and $L^\perp$ is the $-1$-eigenspace.

 None of this required any computations, but we can verify our conclusions using algebra. First we compute the matrix $A$:

$$T\vec{1 0} = \vec{0 -1} \qquad
 T\vec{0 1} = \vec{-1 0} \quad\implies\quad
 A = \mat{0 -1; -1 0}.$$

 Computing the $1$-eigenspace means solving the matrix equation $(A-I_2)v=0$. We have

$$A-I_2 = \mat{0 -1; -1 0} - \mat{1 0; 0 1} = \mat{-1 -1; -1 -1}
 \quad\xrightarrow{\text{RREF}}\quad\mat{1 1; 0 0}.$$

 The parametric form of the solution set is $x = -y$, or equivalently, $y = -x$, which is exactly the equation for $L$. Computing the $-1$-eigenspace means solving the matrix equation $(A+I_2)v=0$; we have

$$A+I_2 = \mat{0 -1; -1 0} + \mat{1 0; 0 1} = \mat{1 -1; -1 1}
 \quad\xrightarrow{\text{RREF}}\quad\mat{1 -1; 0 0}.$$

 The parametric form of the solution set is $x = y$, or equivalently, $y = x$, which is exactly the equation for $L^\perp$.

 The violet line $L$ is the $1$-eigenspace, and the green line $L^\perp$ is the $-1$-eigenspace.

nodes.title: evecs-eval0
nodes.body:
Let $A$ be an $n\times n$ matrix.

 The number $0$ is an eigenvalue of $A$ if and only if $A$ is not invertible.

 In this case, the $0$-eigenspace of $A$ is $\Nul(A)$.

nodes.title: Proof: evecs-eval0
nodes.body: We know that $0$ is an eigenvalue of $A$ if and only if $\Nul(A - 0I_n) = \Nul(A)$ is nonzero, which is equivalent to the noninvertibility of $A$ by the [imt-1]. In this case, the $0$-eigenspace is by definition $\Nul(A-0I_n) = \Nul(A)$.

nodes.title: The Invertible Matrix Theorem: Addenda
nodes.body: We now have two new ways of saying that a matrix is invertible, so we add them to the [imt-1].

nodes.title: imt-2
nodes.body:
Let $A$ be an $n\times n$ matrix, and let $T\colon\R^n\to\R^n$ be the matrix transformation $T(x) = Ax$. The following statements are equivalent:

$A$ is invertible.

$A$ has $n$ pivots.

$\Nul(A) = \{0\}$.

The columns of $A$ are linearly independent.

The columns of $A$ span $\R^n$.

$Ax=b$ has a unique solution for each $b$ in $\R^n$.

$T$ is invertible.

$T$ is one-to-one.

$T$ is onto.

$\det(A) \neq 0$.

$0$ is not an eigenvalue of $A$.

nodes.title: Systems of Linear Equations: Algebra
Systems of Linear Equations: Geometry
nodes.body:
We have already discussed systems of linear equations and how this is related to matrices. In this chapter we will learn how to write a system of linear equations succinctly as a matrix equation, which looks like $Ax=b$, where $A$ is an $m \times n$ matrix, $b$ is a vector in $\R^m$ and $x$ is a variable vector in $\R^n$. As we will see, this is a powerful perspective. We will study two related questions:

What is the set of solutions to $Ax=b$?

What is the set of $b$ so that $Ax=b$ is consistent?

 The first question is the kind you are used to from your first algebra class: what is the set of solutions to $x^2-1=0$. The second is also something you could have studied in your previous algebra classes: for which $b$ does $x^2=b$ have a solution? This question is more subtle at first glance, but you can solve it in the same way as the first question, with the quadratic formula.

 In order to answer the two questions listed above, we will use geometry. This will be analogous to how you used parabolas in order to understand the solutions to a quadratic equation in one variable. Specifically, this chapter is devoted to the geometric study of two objects:

the solution set of a matrix equation $Ax=b$, and

the set of all $b$ that makes a particular system consistent.

 The second object will be called the column space of $A$. The two objects are related in a beautiful way by the rank theorem in [rank-thm].

 Instead of parabolas and hyperbolas, our geometric objects are subspaces, such as lines and planes. Our geometric objects will be something like 13-dimensional planes in $\R^{27}$, etc. It is amazing that we can say anything substantive about objects that we cannot directly visualize. 

 We will develop a large amount of vocabulary that we will use to describe the above objects: vectors ([vectors]), spans ([spans]), linear independence ([linear-independence]), subspaces ([subspaces]), dimension ([dimension]),

 coordinate systems ([bases-as-coord-systems]),

 etc. We will use these concepts to give a precise geometric description of the solution set of any system of equations ([solution-sets]). We will also learn how to express systems of equations more simply using matrix equations ([matrix-equations]).

nodes.title: Linear Transformations and Matrix Algebra
nodes.body:
Learn about linear transformations and their relationship to matrices.

 In practice, one is often lead to ask questions about the geometry of a transformation: a function that takes an input and produces an output. This kind of question can be answered by linear algebra if the transformation can be expressed by a matrix.

 Suppose you are building a robot arm with three joints that can move its hand around a plane, as in the following picture.

 Unfortunately, this kind of function does not come from a matrix, so one cannot use linear algebra to answer questions about this function. In fact, these functions are rather complicated; their study is the subject of inverse kinematics.

 In this chapter, we will be concerned with the relationship between matrices and transformations. In [matrix-transformations], we will consider the equation $b = Ax$ as a function with independent variable $x$ and dependent variable $b$, and we draw pictures accordingly. We spend some time studying transformations in the abstract, and asking questions about a transformation, like whether it is one-to-one and/or onto ([one-to-one-onto]). In [linear-transformations] we will answer the question: when exactly can a transformation be expressed by a matrix? We then present matrix multiplication as a special case of composition of transformations ([matrix-multiplication]). This leads to the study of matrix algebra: that is, to what extent one can do arithmetic with matrices in the place of numbers. With this in place, we learn to solve matrix equations by dividing by a matrix in [matrix-inverses].

nodes.title: Determinants
nodes.body:
We begin by recalling the overall structure of this book:

Solve the matrix equation $Ax=b$.

Solve the matrix equation $Ax=\lambda x$, where $\lambda$ is a number.

Approximately solve the matrix equation $Ax=b$.

 At this point we have said all that we will say about the first part. This chapter belongs to the second.

 Learn about determinants: their computation and their properties.

 The determinant of a square matrix $A$ is a number $\det(A)$. This incredible quantity is one of the most important invariants of a matrix; as such, it forms the basis of most advanced computations involving matrices.

 In [determinants-definitions-properties], we will define the determinant in terms of its behavior with respect to row operations. The determinant satisfies many wonderful properties: for instance, $\det(A) \neq 0$ if and only if $A$ is invertible. We will discuss some of these properties in [determinants-definitions-properties] as well.
 In [determinants-cofactors], we will give a recursive formula for the determinant of a matrix. This formula is very useful, for instance, when taking the determinant of a matrix with unknown entries; this will be important in [chap-eigenvalues].
 Finally, in [determinants-volumes], we will relate determinants to volumes. This gives a geometric interpretation for determinants, and explains why the determinant is defined the way it is. This interpretation of determinants is a crucial ingredient in the change-of-variables formula in multivariable calculus.

nodes.title: Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors
nodes.body:
Solve the matrix equation $Ax=\lambda x.$

 This chapter constitutes the core of any first course on linear algebra: eigenvalues and eigenvectors play a crucial role in most real-world applications of the subject.

 In a population of rabbits,

half of the newborn rabbits survive their first year;

of those, half survive their second year;

the maximum life span is three years;

rabbits produce 0, 6, 8 baby rabbits in their first, second, and third years, respectively.

 What is the asymptotic behavior of this system? What will the rabbit population look like in 100 years?

 Left: the population of rabbits in a given year. Right: the proportions of rabbits in that year. Choose any values you like for the starting population, and click Advance 1 year several times. What do you notice about the long-term behavior of the ratios? This phenomenon turns out to be due to eigenvectors.

 In [eigenvectors], we will define eigenvalues and eigenvectors, and show how to compute the latter; in [characteristic-polynomial] we will learn to compute the former.

 In [similarity] we introduce the notion of similar matrices, and demonstrate that similar matrices do indeed behave similarly. In [diagonalization] we study matrices that are similar to diagonal matrices and in [complex-eigenvalues] we study matrices that are similar to rotation-scaling matrices, thus gaining a solid geometric understanding of large classes of matrices. Finally, we spend [stochastic-matrices] presenting a common kind of application of eigenvalues and eigenvectors to real-world problems, including searching the Internet using Googles PageRank algorithm.

 In [diagonalization] we will use eigenvalues and eigenvectors to determine when a matrix is similar to a diagonal matrix, and we will see that the algebra and geometry of such a matrix is much simpler to understand.
Finally, we spend [stochastic-matrices] presenting a common kind of application of eigenvalues and eigenvectors to real-world problems, including searching the Internet using Googles PageRank algorithm.

nodes.title: Orthogonality
Dot Products and Orthogonality
The Dot Product
nodes.body:
The basic construction in this section is the dot product, which measures angles between vectors and computes the length of a vector.

 For example,

$$\vec{1 2 3}\cdot\vec{4 5 6} = \mat{1 2 3}\vec{4 5 6}
 = 1\cdot 4 + 2\cdot 5 + 3\cdot 6 = 32.$$

 Notice that the dot product of two vectors is a scalar.

 You can do arithmetic with dot products mostly as usual, as long as you remember you can only dot two vectors together, and that the result is a scalar.

 The dot product of a vector with itself is an important special case:

$$\vec{x_1 x_2 \vdots, x_n}\cdot\vec{x_1 x_2 \vdots, x_n}
 = x_1^2 + x_2^2 + \cdots + x_n^2.$$

 Therefore, for any vector $x$, we have:

$x\cdot x \geq 0$

$x\cdot x = 0 \iff x = 0.$

 This leads to a good definition of length.

 It is easy to see why this is true for vectors in $\R^2$, by the Pythagorean theorem.

\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=1,decoration={brace,raise=3pt}]
 \draw[grid lines] (0,0) grid (5,5);
 \point at (0,0);
 \point["$\vec{3 4}$" right] (x) at (3,4);
 \draw[vector] (0,0)
 -- node[sloped,above,inner sep=1pt] {$\sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5$}
 (x);
 \draw[decorate,decoration={mirror}] (0,0) -- node[below=4pt] {3} (3,0);
 \draw[decorate] (0,0) -- node[left=3pt] {4} (0,4);

 \node at (8,2.5) {$\left\|\vec{3 4}\right\| = \sqrt{3^2+4^2} = 5$};

\end{tikzpicture}

 For vectors in $\R^3$, one can check that $\|x\|$ really is the length of $x$, although now this requires two applications of the Pythagorean theorem.

 Note that the length of a vector is the length of the arrow; if we think in terms of points, then the length is its distance from the origin.

 This says that scaling a vector by $c$ scales its length by $|c|$. For example,

$$\left\|\vec{6 8}\right\| = \left\|2\vec{3 4}\right\|
 = 2\left\|\vec{3 4}\right\| = 10.$$

 Now that we have a good notion of length, we can define the distance between points in $\R^n$. Recall that the difference between two points $x,y$ is naturally a vector, namely, the vector $y-x$ pointing from $x$ to $y$.

 Vectors with length $1$ are very common in applications, so we give them a name.

 The [defn-standard-coord-vectors] $e_1,e_2,e_3,\ldots$ are unit vectors:

$$\|e_1\| = \left\|\vec{1 0 0}\right\| = \sqrt{1^2 + 0^2 + 0^2} = 1.$$

 For any nonzero vector $x$, there is a unique unit vector pointing in the same direction. It is obtained by dividing by the length of $x$.

 This is in fact a unit vector (noting that $\|x\|$ is a positive number, so $\bigl|1/\|x\|\bigr| = 1/\|x\|$):

$$\left\|\frac{x}{\|x\|}\right\| = \frac 1{\|x\|}\|x\| = 1.$$

nodes.title: dot product
nodes.body:
x\cdot yDot product of two vectors

 The dot product of two vectors $x,y$ in $\R^n$ is

$$x\cdot y = \vec{x_1 x_2 \vdots, x_n} \cdot \vec{y_1 y_2 \vdots, y_n}
 \;=\; x_1y_1 + x_2y_2 + \cdots + x_ny_n.$$

 Thinking of $x,y$ as column vectors, this is the same as $x^Ty$.

nodes.title: length
nodes.body:
The length of a vector $x$ in $\R^n$ is the number

$$\|x\| = \sqrt{x\cdot x} = \sqrt{x_1^2 + x_2^2 + \cdots + x_n^2}.$$

nodes.title: innerprod-example-1
nodes.body:
Suppose that $\|x\| = 2,\;\|y\|=3,$ and $x\cdot y = -4$. What is $\|2x + 3y\|$?

 We compute

$$\begin{split}
 \|2x+3y\|^2 &= (2x+3y)\cdot(2x+3y) \\
 &= 4x\cdot x + 6x\cdot y + 6x\cdot y + 9y\cdot y \\
 &= 4\|x\|^2 + 9\|y\|^2 + 12x\cdot y \\
 &= 4\cdot 4 + 9\cdot 9 - 12\cdot 4 = 49.
 \end{split}$$

 Hence $\|2x+3y\| = \sqrt{49} = 7.$

nodes.title: innerprod-fact-2
nodes.body: If $x$ is a vector and $c$ is a scalar, then $\|cx\|=|c|\cdot\|x\|.$

nodes.title: distance
nodes.body:
The distance between two points $x,y$ in $\R^n$ is the length of the [vectors-diff-pts] $x$ to $y$:

$$\dist(x,y) = \|y-x\|.$$

nodes.title: innerprod-example-2
unit vector
nodes.body: A unit vector is a vector $x$ with length $\|x\| = \sqrt{x\cdot x} =1$.

nodes.title: unit vector in the direction of x
nodes.body: Let $x$ be a nonzero vector in $\R^n$. The unit vector in the direction of $x$ is the vector $x/\|x\|$.

nodes.title: innerprod-example-3
Orthogonal Vectors
orthogonal
nodes.body: Two vectors $x,y$ in $\R^n$ are orthogonal or perpendicular if $x\cdot y = 0$.

nodes.title: innerprod-example-4
nodes.body:
Find all vectors orthogonal to $v = \vec{1 1 -1}.$

 We have to find all vectors $x$ such that $x\cdot v = 0$. This means solving the equation

$$0 = x\cdot v = \vec{x_1 x_2 x_3}\cdot\vec{1 1 -1} = x_1 + x_2 - x_3.$$

 The parametric form for the solution set is $x_1 = -x_2 + x_3$, so the parametric vector form of the general solution is

$$x = \vec{x_1 x_2 x_3} = x_2\vec{-1 1 0} + x_3\vec{1 0 1}.$$

 Therefore, the answer is the plane

$$\Span\left\{\vec{-1 1 0},\;\vec{1 0 1}\right\}.$$

 For instance,

$$\vec{-1 1 0}\perp\vec{1 1 -1} \sptxt{because} \vec{-1 1 0}\cdot\vec{1 1 -1} = 0$$
.

nodes.title: innerprod-example-5
nodes.body:
Find all vectors orthogonal to both $v = \vec{1 1 -1}$ and $w = \vec{1 1 1}$.

 We have to solve the system of two homogeneous equations

$$\spalignsysdelims..
 \syseq{
 0 = x\cdot v = \vec{x_1 x_2 x_3}\cdot\vec{1 1 -1} = x_1 + x_2 - x_3;
 0 = x\cdot w = \vec{x_1 x_2 x_3}\cdot\vec{1 1 1} = x_1 + x_2 + x_3\rlap.}$$

 In matrix form:

$$\mat{1 1 -1; 1 1 1} \;\xrightarrow{\text{RREF}}\;\mat{1 1 0; 0 0 1}.$$

 The parametric vector form of the solution set is

$$\vec{x_1 x_2 x_3} = x_2\vec{-1 1 0}.$$

 Therefore, the answer is the line

$$\Span\left\{\vec{-1 1 0}\right\}.$$

 For instance,

$$\vec{-1 1 0}\cdot\vec{1 1 -1} = 0 \sptxt{and}
 \vec{-1 1 0}\cdot\vec{1 1 1} = 0.$$

nodes.title: Angle between two vectors
nodes.body:
More generally, the law of cosines gives a formula for the angle $\alpha$ between two nonzero vectors:

$$\begin{split}
 2\|x\|\|y\|\cos(\alpha)
 \amp= \|x\|^2 + \|y\|^2 - \|y-x\|^2 \\
 \amp= x\cdot x + y\cdot y - (y-x)\cdot (y-x) \\
 \amp= x\cdot x + y\cdot y - y\cdot y - x\cdot x + 2x\cdot y \\
 \amp= 2x\cdot y \\
 \amp\quad\implies \alpha = \cos\inv\left(\frac{x\cdot y}{\|x\|\|y\|}\right).
 \end{split}$$

 In higher dimensions, we take this to be the definition of the angle between $x$ and $y$.

nodes.title: The Invertible Matrix Theorem
nodes.body:
Theorem: the invertible matrix theorem.

This section consists of a single important theorem containing many equivalent conditions for a matrix to be invertible. This is one of the most important theorems in this textbook. We will append two more criteria in [eigenvectors].

 To reiterate, the invertible matrix theorem means:

 The reader should be comfortable translating any of the statements in the invertible matrix theorem into a statement about the pivots of a matrix.

 Now we can show that to check $B = A\inv$, it's enough to show $AB=I_n$ or $BA=I_n$.

 We conclude with some common situations in which the invertible matrix theorem is useful.

nodes.title: imt-1
nodes.body:
Let $A$ be an $n\times n$ matrix, and let $T\colon\R^n\to\R^n$ be the matrix transformation $T(x) = Ax$. The following statements are equivalent:

$A$ is invertible.

$A$ has $n$ pivots.

$\Nul(A) = \{0\}$.

The columns of $A$ are linearly independent.

The columns of $A$ span $\R^n$.

$Ax=b$ has a unique solution for each $b$ in $\R^n$.

$T$ is invertible.

$T$ is one-to-one.

$T$ is onto.

nodes.title: Proof: imt-1
nodes.body:
$(1\iff 2)$: The matrix $A$ has $n$ pivots if and only if its reduced row echelon form is the identity matrix $I_n$. This happens exactly when the [matrix-inv-how-to-compute] to compute the inverse succeeds.

 $(2\iff 3)$:
 The null space of a matrix is $\{0\}$ if and only if the matrix has no free variables, which means that every column is a pivot column, which means $A$ has $n$ pivots. See this [subspaces-span-nullspace].

 $(2\iff 4,\,2\iff 5)$:
 These follow from this [linindep-matrix-cols] and this [matrixeq-thm-full-span], respectively, since $A$ has $n$ pivots if and only if has a pivot in every row/column.

 $(4+5\iff 6)$:
 We know $Ax=b$ has at least one solution for every $b$ if and only if the columns of $A$ span $\R^n$ by this [matrix-trans-onto], and $Ax=b$ has at most one solution for every $b$ if and only if the columns of $A$ are linearly independent by this [matrix-trans-one-to-one]. Hence $Ax=b$ has exactly one solution for every $b$ if and only if its columns are linearly independent and span $\R^n$.

 $(1\iff 7)$:
 This is the content of this [matrix-inv-matrix-inv-comp].

 $(7\implies 8+9)$:
 See this [matrix-inv-11-onto].

 $(8\iff 4,\,9\iff 5)$:
 See this this [matrix-trans-one-to-one] and this [matrix-trans-onto].

nodes.title: Other Conditions for Invertibility
nodes.body:
The following conditions are also equivalent to the invertibility of a square matrix $A$. They are all simple restatements of conditions in the invertible matrix theorem.

The reduced row echelon form of $A$ is the identity matrix $I_n$.

$Ax=0$ has no solutions other than the trivial one.

$\nullity(A) = 0$.

The columns of $A$ form a basis for $\R^n$.

$Ax=b$ is consistent for all $b$ in $\R^n$.

$\Col(A) = \R^n.$

$\dim\Col(A) = n.$

$\rank(A) = n.$

nodes.title: A Left or Right Inverse Suffices
nodes.body: Let $A$ be an $n\times n$ matrix, and suppose that there exists an $n\times n$ matrix $B$ such that $AB=I_n$ or $BA=I_n$. Then $A$ is invertible and $B = A\inv$.

nodes.title: Proof: A Left or Right Inverse Suffices
nodes.body:
Suppose that $AB = I_n$. We claim that $T(x)=Ax$ is onto. Indeed, for any $b$ in $\R^n$, we have

$$b = I_nb = (AB)b = A(Bb),$$

 so $T(Bb) = b$, and hence $b$ is in the range of $T$. Therefore, $A$ is invertible by the [imt-1]. Since $A$ is invertible, we have

$$A\inv = A\inv I_n = A\inv (AB) = (A\inv A)B = I_n B = B,$$

 so $B = A\inv.$

 Now suppose that $BA = I_n$. We claim that $T(x) = Ax$ is one-to-one. Indeed, suppose that $T(x) = T(y)$. Then $Ax = Ay$, so $BAx = BAy$. But $BA = I_n$, so $I_nx = I_ny$, and hence $x=y$. Therefore, $A$ is invertible by the [imt-1]. One shows that $B = A\inv$ as above.

nodes.title: invertible-matrix-thm-example-1
nodes.body:
Is this matrix invertible?

$$A = \mat{1 2 -1; 2 4 7; -2 -4 1}$$

 The second column is a multiple of the first. The columns are linearly dependent, so $A$ does not satisfy condition 4 of the [imt-1]. Therefore, $A$ is not invertible.

nodes.title: invertible-matrix-thm-example-2
nodes.body:
Let $A$ be an $n\times n$ matrix and let $T(x) = Ax$. Suppose that the range of $T$ is $\R^n$. Show that the columns of $A$ are linearly independent.

 The range of $T$ is the column space of $A$, so $A$ satisfies condition 5 of the [imt-1]. Therefore, $A$ also satisfies condition 4, which says that the columns of $A$ are linearly independent.

nodes.title: invertible-matrix-thm-example-3
nodes.body:
Let $A$ be a $3\times 3$ matrix such that

$$A\vec{1 7 0} = A\vec{2 0 -1}.$$

 Show that the rank of $A$ is at most $2$.

 If we set

$$b = A\vec{1 7 0} = A\vec{2 0 -1},$$

 then $Ax=b$ has multiple solutions, so it does not satisfy condition 6 of the [imt-1]. Therefore, it does not satisfy condition 5, so the columns of $A$ do not span $\R^3$. Therefore, the column space has dimension strictly less than 3, the rank is at most $2$.

nodes.title: invertible-matrix-thm-example-4
nodes.body:
Suppose that $A$ is an $n\times n$ matrix such that $Ax=b$ is inconsistent some vector $b$. Show that $Ax=b$ has infinitely many solutions for some (other) vector $b$.

 By hypothesis, $A$ does not satisfy condition 6 of the [imt-1]. Therefore, it does not satisfy condition $3$, so $\Nul(A)$ is an infinite set. If we take $b=0$, then the equation $Ax=b$ has infinitely many solutions.

nodes.title: The Method of Least Squares
nodes.body:
Learn examples of best-fit problems.

Learn to turn a best-fit problem into a least-squares problem.

Recipe: find a least-squares

 solution (two ways).

 solution.

Picture: geometry of a least-squares solution.

Vocabulary words: least-squares solution.

 In this section, we answer the following important question:

 Suppose that $Ax=b$ does not have a solution. What is the best approximate solution?

 For our purposes, the best approximate solution is called the least-squares solution. We will present two methods for finding least-squares solutions, and we will give several applications to best-fit problems.

nodes.title: Least-Squares Solutions
least-squares solution
nodes.body:
Let $A$ be an $m\times n$ matrix and let $b$ be a vector in $\R^m$. A least-squares solution of the matrix equation $Ax=b$ is a vector $\hat x$ in $\R^n$ such that

$$\dist(b,\,A\hat x) \leq \dist(b,\,Ax)$$

 for all other vectors $x$ in $\R^n$.

nodes.title: leastsquares-ATA-method
nodes.body:
Let $A$ be an $m\times n$ matrix and let $b$ be a vector in $\R^m$. The least-squares solutions of $Ax=b$ are the solutions of the matrix equation

$$A^TAx = A^Tb$$

nodes.title: Proof: leastsquares-ATA-method
nodes.body: By this [projections-ATA-formula], if $\hat x$ is a solution of the matrix equation $A^TAx = A^Tb$, then $A\hat x$ is equal to $b_{\Col(A)}$. We argued above that a least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ is a solution of $Ax = b_{\Col(A)}.$

nodes.title: leastsquares-eg-bestfit-line-a
leastsquares-example-2
nodes.body:
Find the least-squares solutions of $Ax=b$ where:

$$A = \mat[r]{2 0; -1 1; 0 2} \qquad b = \vec[r]{1 0 -1}.$$

 We have

$$A^T A = \mat[r]{2 -1 0; 0 1 2}\mat[r]{2 0; -1 1; 0 2} =
 \mat[r]{5 -1; -1 5}$$

 and

$$A^T b = \mat[r]{2 -1 0; 0 1 2}\vec[r]{1 0 -1}
 = \vec[r]{2 -2}.$$

 We form an augmented matrix and row reduce:

$$\amat{5 -1 2; -1 5 -2} \rref \amat{1 0 1/3; 0 1 -1/3}.$$

 Therefore, the only least-squares solution is $\hat x = \frac 13{1\choose -1}.$

 The red plane is $\Col(A)$. The closest that $Ax$ can get to $b$ is the closest vector on $\Col(A)$ to $b$, which is the orthogonal projection $b_{\Col(A)}$ (in blue). The vectors $v_1,v_2$ are the columns of $A$, and the coefficients of $\hat x$ are the

 $\cB$-coordinates of $b_{\Col(A)}$, where $\cB = \{v_1,v_2\}$.

 lengths of the green lines.

nodes.title: leastsquares-theorem-2
nodes.body:
Let $A$ be an $m\times n$ matrix and let $b$ be a vector in $\R^m$. The following are equivalent:

$Ax=b$ has a unique least-squares solution.

The columns of $A$ are linearly independent.

$A^TA$ is invertible.

 In this case, the least-squares solution is

$$\hat x = (A^TA)\inv A^Tb.$$

nodes.title: Proof: leastsquares-theorem-2
nodes.body: The set of least-squares solutions of $Ax=b$ is the solution set of the consistent equation $A^TAx=A^Tb$, which is a translate of the solution set of the homogeneous equation $A^TAx=0$. Since $A^TA$ is a square matrix, the equivalence of 1 and 3 follows from the [imt-2]. The set of least squares-solutions is also the solution set of the consistent equation $Ax = b_{\Col(A)}$, which has a unique solution if and only if the columns of $A$ are linearly independent by this [linindep-matrix-cols].

nodes.title: Infinitely many least-squares solutions
leastsquares-example-4
Best-Fit Problems
nodes.body:
In this subsection we give an application of the method of least squares to data modeling. We begin with a basic example.

 All of the above examples have the following form: some number of data points $(x,y)$ are specified, and we want to find a function

$$y = B_1g_1(x) + B_2g_2(x) + \cdots + B_mg_m(x)$$

 that best approximates these points, where $g_1,g_2,\ldots,g_m$ are fixed functions of $x$. Indeed, in the best-fit line example we had $g_1(x)=x$ and $g_2(x)=1$; in the best-fit parabola example we had $g_1(x)=x^2$, $g_2(x)=x$, and $g_3(x)=1$; and in the best-fit linear function example we had $g_1(x_1,x_2)=x_1$, $g_2(x_1,x_2)=x_2$, and $g_3(x_1,x_2)=1$ (in this example we take $x$ to be a vector with two entries). We evaluate the above equation on the given data points to obtain a system of linear equations in the unknowns $B_1,B_2,\ldots,B_m$once we evaluate the $g_i$, they just become numbers, so it does not matter what they areand we find the least-squares solution. The resulting best-fit function minimizes the sum of the squares of the vertical distances from the graph of $y = f(x)$ to our original data points.

 To emphasize that the nature of the functions $g_i$ really is irrelevant, consider the following example.

 The next example has a somewhat different flavor from the previous ones.

nodes.title: Interactive: Best-fit line
nodes.body: The best-fit line minimizes the sum of the squares of the vertical distances (violet). Click and drag the points to see how the best-fit line changes.

nodes.title: Best-fit parabola
Best-fit linear function
Best-fit trigonometric function
Best-fit ellipse
Linear Transformations
nodes.body:
Learn how to verify that a transformation is linear, or prove that a transformation is not linear.

Understand the relationship between linear transformations and matrix transformations.

Recipe: compute the matrix of a linear transformation.

Theorem: linear transformations and matrix transformations.

Notation: the standard coordinate vectors $e_1,e_2,\ldots$.

Vocabulary words: linear transformation, standard matrix, identity matrix.

 In [matrix-transformations], we studied the geometry of matrices by regarding them as functions, i.e., by considering the associated matrix transformations. We defined some vocabulary (domain, codomain, range), and asked a number of natural questions about a transformation. For a matrix transformation, these translate into questions about matrices, which we have many tools to answer.

 In this section, we make a change in perspective. Suppose that we are given a transformation that we would like to study. If we can prove that our transformation is a matrix transformation, then we can use linear algebra to study it. This raises two important questions:

 How can we tell if a transformation is a matrix transformation?

 If our transformation is a matrix transformation, how do we find its matrix?

 For example, we saw in this [matrix-trans-eg-rotation] that the matrix transformation

$$T\colon\R^2\To\R^2 \qquad T(x) = \mat{0 -1; 1 0}x$$

 is a counterclockwise rotation of the plane by $90^\circ$. However, we could have defined $T$ in this way:

$$T\colon\R^2\To\R^2 \qquad T(x) = \text{the counterclockwise rotation of $x$ by $90^\circ$}.$$

 Given this definition, it is not at all obvious that $T$ is a matrix transformation, or what matrix it is associated to.

nodes.title: Linear Transformations: Definition
nodes.body:
In this section, we introduce the class of transformations that come from matrices.

 Let $T\colon\R^n\to\R^m$ be a matrix transformation: $T(x)=Ax$ for an $m\times n$ matrix $A$. By this [matrix-linearity], we have

$$\begin{aligned}T(u + v) = A(u + v) &= Au + Av = T(u) + T(v) \\ T(cu) = A(cu) &= cAu = cT(u)\end{aligned}$$

 for all vectors $u,v$ in $\R^n$ and all scalars $c$. Since a matrix transformation satisfies the two defining properties, it is a linear transformation

 We will see in the next [linear-trans-is-matrix-trans] that the opposite is true: every linear transformation is a matrix transformation; we just haven't computed its matrix yet.

 In engineering, the second fact is called the superposition principle; it should remind you of the distributive property.
 For example, $T(cu + dv) = cT(u) + dT(v)$ for any vectors $u,v$ and any scalars $c,d$. To restate the first fact:

 One can show that, if a transformation is defined by formulas in the coordinates as in the above example, then the transformation is linear if and only if each coordinate is a linear expression in the variables with no constant term.

 When deciding whether a transformation $T$ is linear, generally the first thing to do is to check whether $T(0)=0$; if not, $T$ is automatically not linear. Note however that the non-linear transformations $T_1$ and $T_2$ of the above example do take the zero vector to the zero vector.

nodes.title: linear transformation
nodes.body:
A linear transformation is a transformation $T\colon\R^n\to\R^m$ satisfying

$$\begin{aligned}T(u + v) &= T(u) + T(v) \\ T(cu) &= cT(u)\end{aligned}$$

 for all vectors $u,v$ in $\R^n$ and all scalars $c$.

nodes.title: Facts about linear transformations
nodes.body:
Let $T\colon\R^n\to\R^m$ be a linear transformation. Then:

 $T(0)=0$.

 For any vectors $v_1,v_2,\ldots,v_k$ in $\R^n$ and scalars $c_1,c_2,\ldots,c_k$, we have

$$T\bigl( c_1v_1 + c_2v_2 + \cdots + c_kv_k \bigr)
 = c_1 T(v_1) + c_2 T(v_2) + \cdots + c_k T(v_k).$$

nodes.title: Proof: Facts about linear transformations
A non-linear transformation
nodes.body:
Define $T\colon\R\to\R$ by $T(x) = x+1$. Is $T$ a linear transformation?

 We have $T(0) = 0 + 1 = 1$. Since any linear transformation necessarily takes zero to zero by the above [linear-trans-T0-0], we conclude that $T$ is not linear (even though its graph is a line).

 Note: in this case, it was not necessary to check explicitly that $T$ does not satisfy both [linear-trans-defn]: since $T(0)=0$ is a consequence of these properties, at least one of them must not be satisfied. (In fact, this $T$ satisfies neither.)

nodes.title: Verifying linearity: dilation
nodes.body:
Define $T\colon\R^2\to\R^2$ by $T(x)=1.5x$. Verify that $T$ is linear.

 We have to check the [linear-trans-defn] for all vectors $u,v$ and all scalars $c$. In other words, we have to treat $u,v,$ and $c$ as unknowns. The only thing we are allowed to use is the definition of $T$.

$$\begin{aligned}
 T(u + v) &= 1.5(u + v) = 1.5u + 1.5v = T(u) + T(v)
 \\ 
 T(cu) &= 1.5(cu) = c(1.5u) = cT(u).
 \end{aligned}$$

 Since $T$ satisfies both defining properties, $T$ is linear.

 Note: we know from this [matrix-trans-eg-dilation] that $T$ is a matrix transformation: in fact,

$$T(x) = \mat{1.5 0; 0 1.5}x.$$

 Since a matrix transformation is a linear transformation, this is another proof that $T$ is linear.

nodes.title: Verifying linearity: rotation
A transformation defined by a formula
nodes.body:
Define $T\colon\R^2\to\R^3$ by the formula

$$T\vec{x y} = \vec{3x-y y x}.$$

 Verify that $T$ is linear.

 We have to check the [linear-trans-defn] for all vectors $u,v$ and all scalars $c$. In other words, we have to treat $u,v,$ and $c$ as unknowns; the only thing we are allowed to use is the definition of $T$. Since $T$ is defined in terms of the coordinates of $u,v$, we need to give those names as well; say $u={x_1\choose y_1}$ and $v={x_2\choose y_2}$. For the first property, we have

$$\begin{split}
 T\left(\vec{x_1 y_1} + \vec{x_2 y_2}\right)
 &= T\vec{x_1+x_2 y_1+y_2}
 = \vec{3(x_1+x_2)-(y_1+y_2) y_1+y_2 x_1+x_2} \\
 &= \vec{(3x_1-y_1)+(3x_2-y_2) y_1+y_2 x_1+x_2} \\
 &= \vec{3x_1-y_1 y_1 x_1} + \vec{3x_2-y_2 y_2 x_2}
 = T\vec{x_1 y_1} + T\vec{x_2 y_2}.
 \end{split}$$

 For the second property,

$$\begin{split}
 T\left(c\vec{x_1 y_1}\right)
 &= T\vec{cx_1 cy_1}
 = \vec{3(cx_1)-(cy_1) cy_1 cx_1} \\
 &= \vec{c(3x_1-y_1) cy_1 cx_1}
 = c\vec{3x_1-y_1 y_1 x_1}
 = cT\vec{x_1 y_1}.
 \end{split}$$

 Since $T$ satisfies the [linear-trans-defn], $T$ is a linear transformation.

 Note: we will see in this [linear-trans-matrix-formula] below that

$$T\vec{x y} = \mat{3 -1; 0 1; 1 0}\vec{x y}.$$

 Hence $T$ is in fact a matrix transformation.

nodes.title: A translation
nodes.body:
Define $T\colon\R^3\to\R^3$ by

$$T(x) = x + \vec{1 2 3}.$$

 This kind of transformation is called a translation.
 As in a previous [linear-trans-eg-T0-non0], this $T$
 is not linear, because $T(0)$ is not the zero vector.

nodes.title: More non-linear transformations
nodes.body:
Verify that the following transformations from $\R^2$ to $\R^2$ are not linear:

$$T_1\vec{x y} = \vec{|x| y} \qquad
 T_2\vec{x y} = \vec{xy y} \qquad
 T_3\vec{x y} = \vec{2x+1 x-2y}.$$

 In order to verify that a transformation $T$ is not linear, we have to show that $T$ does not satisfy at least one of the two [linear-trans-defn]. For the first, the negation of the statement $T(u+v)=T(u)+T(v)$ for all vectors $u,v$ is there exists at least one pair of vectors $u,v$ such that $T(u+v)\neq T(u)+T(v)$. In other words, it suffices to find one example of a pair of vectors $u,v$ such that $T(u+v)\neq T(u)+T(v)$. Likewise, for the second, the negation of the statement $T(cu) = cT(u)$ for all vectors $u$ and all scalars $c$ is there exists some vector $u$ and some scalar $c$ such that $T(cu)\neq cT(u)$. In other words, it suffices to find one vector $u$ and one scalar $c$ such that $T(cu)\neq cT(u)$.

 For the first transformation, we note that

$$T_1\left(-\vec{1 0}\right) = T_1\vec{-1 0} = \vec{|-1| 0} = \vec{1 0}$$

 but that

$$-T_1\vec{1 0} = -\vec{|1| 0} = -\vec{1 0} = \vec{-1 0}.$$

 Therefore, this transformation does not satisfy the second property.

 For the second transformation, we note that

$$T_2\left(2\vec{1 1}\right) = T_2\vec{2 2} = \vec{2\cdot 2 2} = \vec{4 2}$$

 but that

$$2T_2\vec{1 1} = 2\vec{1\cdot 1 1} = 2\vec{1 1} = \vec{2 2}.$$

 Therefore, this transformation does not satisfy the second property.

 For the third transformation, we observe that

$$T_3\vec{0 0} = \vec{2(0)+1 0-2(0)} = \vec{1 0}\neq\vec{0 0}.$$

 Since $T_3$ does not take the zero vector to the zero vector, it cannot be linear.

nodes.title: linear-trans-remark-1
nodes.body: Find an example of a transformation that satisfies the first [linear-trans-defn] but not the second.

nodes.title: The Standard Coordinate Vectors
Multiplying a matrix by the standard coordinate vectors
nodes.body:
If $A$ is an $m\times n$ matrix with columns $v_1,v_2,\ldots,v_m$, then $\color{red}Ae_i = v_i$ for each $i=1,2,\ldots,n$:

$$\mat{| | ,, |; v_1 v_2 \cdots, v_n; | | ,, |}e_i = v_i.$$

 In other words, multiplying a matrix by $e_i$ simply selects its $i$th column.

nodes.title: n\times n identity matrix
The Matrix of a Linear Transformation
nodes.body:
Now we can prove that every linear transformation is a matrix transformation, and we will show how to compute the matrix.

 The matrix $A$ in the above theorem is called the standard matrix for $T$. The columns of $A$ are the vectors obtained by evaluating $T$ on the $n$ standard coordinate vectors in $\R^n$. To summarize part of the theorem:

 We saw in the above example that the matrix for counterclockwise rotation of the plane by an angle of $\theta$ is

$$A = \mat{\cos\theta, -\sin\theta; \sin\theta, \cos\theta}.$$

 Recall from this [matrix-trans-identity] that the identity transformation is the transformation $\Id_{\R^n}\colon\R^n\to\R^n$ defined by $\Id_{\R^n}(x) = x$ for every vector $x$.

 We computed in this [linear-trans-matrix-of-id] that the matrix of the identity transform is the identity matrix: for every $x$ in $\R^n$,

$$x = \Id_{\R^n}(x) = I_nx.$$

 Therefore, $I_nx=x$ for all vectors $x$: the product of the identity matrix and a vector is the same vector.

nodes.title: The matrix of a linear transformation
nodes.body:
Let $T\colon\R^n\to\R^m$ be a linear transformation. Let $A$ be the $m\times n$ matrix

$$A = \mat{| | ,, |; T(e_1) T(e_2) \cdots, T(e_n); | | ,, | }.$$

 Then $T$ is the matrix transformation associated with $A$: that is, $T(x) = Ax$.
nodes.context: The Matrix of a Linear Transformation

nodes.title: Proof: The matrix of a linear transformation
nodes.body:
We suppose for simplicity that $T$ is a transformation from $\R^3$ to $\R^2$. Let $A$ be the matrix given in the statement of the theorem. Then

$$\begin{split}
 T\vec{x y z} \amp;= T\left( x\vec{1 0 0} + y\vec{0 1 0} + z\vec{0 0 1} \right) \\
 \amp= T\bigl( xe_1 + ye_2 + ze_3 \bigr) \\
 \amp= xT(e_1) + yT(e_2) + zT(e_3) \\
 \amp= \mat{| | |; T(e_1) T(e_2) T(e_3); | | |}\vec{x y z}\\
 \amp= A\vec{x y z}.
\end{split}$$

nodes.title: The standard matrix of the identity transformation
nodes.body:
Verify that the identity transformation $\Id_{\R^n}\colon\R^n\to\R^n$ is linear, and compute its standard matrix.

 We verify the two [linear-trans-defn] of linear transformations. Let $u,v$ be vectors in $\R^n$. Then

$$\Id_{\R^n}(u+v) = u+v = \Id_{\R^n}(u) + \Id_{\R^n}(v).$$

 If $c$ is a scalar, then

$$\Id_{\R^n}(cu) = cu = c\Id_{\R^n}(u).$$

 Since $\Id_{\R^n}$ satisfies the two defining properties, it is a linear transformation.

 Now that we know that $\Id_{\R^n}$ is linear, it makes sense to compute its standard matrix.
 For each standard coordinate vector $e_i$, we have $\Id_{R^n}(e_i) = e_i$. In other words, the columns of the standard matrix of $\Id_{\R^n}$ are the standard coordinate vectors, so the standard matrix is the identity matrix

$$I_n = \mat{1 0 \cdots, 0 0; 0 1 \cdots, 0 0;
 \vdots, \vdots, \ddots, \vdots, \vdots;
 0 0 \cdots, 1 0; 0 0 \cdots, 0 1}.$$

nodes.title: Linear Independence
nodes.body:
Understand the concept of linear independence.

Learn two criteria for linear independence.

Understand the relationship between linear independence and pivot columns / free variables.

Recipe: test if a set of vectors is linearly independent / find an equation of linear dependence.

Picture: whether a set of vectors in $\R^2$ or $\R^3$ is linearly independent or not.

Vocabulary words: linear dependence relation / equation of linear dependence.

Essential vocabulary words: linearly independent, linearly dependent.

 Sometimes the span of a set of vectors is smaller than you expect from the
number of vectors, as in the picture below. This means that (at least) one of the vectors is redundant: it can be removed without affecting the span. In the present section, we formalize this idea in the notion of linear independence.

 Pictures of sets of vectors that are linearly dependent. Note that in each case, one vector is in the span of the othersso it doesnt make the span bigger.

nodes.title: The Definition of Linear Independence
nodes.body:
In other words, $\{v_1,v_2,\ldots,v_k\}$ is linearly dependent if there exist numbers $x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_k$, not all equal to zero, such that

$$x_1v_1 + x_2v_2 + \cdots + x_kv_k = 0.$$

 This is called a linear dependence relation or equation of linear dependence.

 The above examples lead to the following recipe.

 (Recall that $Ax=0$ has a nontrivial solution if and only if $A$ has a column without a pivot: see this [solnsets-nontrivial].)

 Suppose that $A$ has more columns than rows. Then $A$ cannot have a pivot in every column (it has at most one pivot per row), so its columns are automatically linearly dependent.

For example, four vectors in $\R^3$ are automatically linearly dependent. Note that a tall matrix may or may not have linearly independent columns.

 With regard to the first fact, note that the zero vector is a multiple of any vector, so it is collinear with any other vector. Hence facts 1 and 2 are consistent with each other.

nodes.title: Checking linear dependence
nodes.body:
Is the set

$$\left\{ \vec{1 1 1},\, \vec{1 -1 2},\, \vec{3 1 4} \right\}$$

 linearly independent?

 Equivalently, we are asking if the homogeneous vector equation

$$x\vec{1 1 1} + y\vec{1 -1 2} + z\vec{3 1 4} = \vec{0 0 0}$$

 has a nontrivial solution. We solve this by forming a matrix and row reducing (we do not augment because of this [solnsets-no-augment]):

$$\mat{1 1 3; 1 -1 1; 1 2 4}
 \quad\xrightarrow{\text{row reduce}}\quad
 \mat{1 0 2; 0 1 1; 0 0 0}$$

 This says $x = -2z$ and $y = -z$. So there exist nontrivial solutions: for instance, taking $z=1$ gives this equation of linear dependence:

$$-2\vec{1 1 1} - \vec{1 -1 2} + \vec{3 1 4} = \vec{0 0 0}.$$

 Move the sliders to solve the homogeneous vector equation in this example. Do you see why the vectors need to be coplanar in order for there to exist a nontrivial solution?

nodes.title: Checking linear independence
nodes.body:
Is the set

$$\left\{ \vec{1 1 -2},\, \vec{1 -1 2},\, \vec{3 1 4} \right\}$$

 linearly independent?

 Equivalently, we are asking if the homogeneous vector equation

$$x\vec{1 1 -2} + y\vec{1 -1 2} + z\vec{3 1 4} = \vec{0 0 0}$$

 has a nontrivial solution. We solve this by forming a matrix and row reducing (we do not augment because of this [solnsets-no-augment]):

$$\mat{1 1 3; 1 -1 1; -2 2 4}
 \quad\xrightarrow{\text{row reduce}}\quad
 \mat{1 0 0; 0 1 0; 0 0 1}$$

 This says $x = y = z = 0$, i.e., the only solution is the trivial solution. We conclude that the set is linearly independent.

 Move the sliders to solve the homogeneous vector equation in this example. Do you see why the vectors would need to be coplanar in order for there to exist a nontrivial solution?

nodes.title: Vector parametric form
nodes.body:
An important observation is that the vectors coming from the parametric vector form of the solution of a matrix equation $Ax=0$ are linearly independent. In this [solnsets-eg-plane] we saw that the solution set of $Ax=0$ for 

$$A = \mat{1 -1 2; -2 2 -4}?$$

is

$$x = \vec{x_1 x_2 x_3} = x_2\vec{1 1 0} + x_3\vec{-2 0 1}.$$

Let's explain why the vectors $(1,1,0)$ and $(-2,0,1)$ are linearly independent. Suppose that

$$\vec{0 0 0} = x_2\vec{1 1 0} + x_3\vec{-2 0 1} = \vec{x_2-2x_3 x_2 x_3}.$$

 Comparing the second and third coordinates, we see that $x_2=x_3=0$. This reasoning will work in any example, since the entries corresponding to the free variables are all equal to 1 or 0, and are only equal to 1 in one of the vectors. This observation forms part of this [dimension-basis-nulspace].

nodes.title: Facts about linear independence
nodes.body:
Two vectors are linearly dependent if and only if they are collinear, i.e., one is a scalar multiple of the other.

Any set containing the zero vector is linearly dependent.

If a subset of $\{v_1,v_2,\ldots,v_k\}$ is linearly dependent, then $\{v_1,v_2,\ldots,v_k\}$ is linearly dependent as well.

nodes.title: Proof: Facts about linear independence
nodes.body:
If $v_1 = cv_2$ then $v_1-cv_2=0$, so $\{v_1,v_2\}$ is linearly dependent. In the other direction, if $x_1v_1+x_2v_2=0$ with $x_1\neq0$ (say), then $v_1 = -\frac{x_2}{x_1}v_2$.

 It is easy to produce a linear dependence relation if one vector is the zero vector: for instance, if $v_1=0$ then

$$1\cdot v_1 + 0\cdot v_2 + \cdots + 0\cdot v_k = 0.$$

 After reordering, we may suppose that $\{v_1,v_2,\ldots,v_r\}$ is linearly dependent, with $r < p$. This means that there is an equation of linear dependence

$$x_1v_1 + x_2v_2 + \cdots + x_rv_r = 0$$
,
 with at least one of $x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_r$ nonzero. This is also an equation of linear dependence among $\{v_1,v_2,\ldots,v_k\}$, since we can take the coefficients of $v_{r+1},\ldots,v_k$ to all be zero.

nodes.title: Criteria for Linear Independence
nodes.body:
In this subsection we give two criteria for a set of vectors to be linearly independent. Keep in mind, however, that the actual [linindep-defn-linindep] is above.

 For example, the set $\bigl\{{1\choose 0},\,{2\choose 0},\,{0\choose 1}\bigr\}$ is linearly dependent, but ${0\choose 1}$ is not in the span of the other two vectors. Also see this [linindep-3d-4vecs] below.

 The previous [linindep-criterion-inspan] makes precise in what sense a set of linearly dependent vectors is redundant.

 We can rephrase this as follows:

nodes.title: linindep-criterion-inspan
nodes.body:
A set of vectors $\{v_1,v_2,\ldots,v_k\}$ is linearly dependent if and only if one of the vectors is in the span of the other ones.

Any such vector may be removed without affecting the span.

nodes.title: Proof: linindep-criterion-inspan
nodes.body:
Suppose, for instance, that $v_3$ is in $\Span\{v_1,v_2,v_4\}$, so we have an equation like

$$v_3 = 2v_1 - \frac 12v_2 + 6v_4.$$

 We can subract $v_3$ from both sides of the equation to get

$$0 = 2v_1 - \frac 12v_2 - v_3 + 6v_4.$$

 This is a linear dependence relation.

 In this case, any linear combination of $v_1,v_2,v_3,v_4$ is already a linear combination of $v_1,v_2,v_4$:

$$\begin{aligned}
 x_1v_1 + x_2v_2 + x_3v_3 + x_4v_4 &=
 x_1v_1 + x_2v_2 + x_3\left(2v_1-\frac 12v_2 + 6v_4\right) + x_4v_4
 \\ 
 &= (x_1+2x_3)v_1 + \left(x_2-\frac 12x_3\right)v_2 + (x_4+6)v_4.
 \end{aligned}$$

 Therefore, $\Span\{v_1,v_2,v_3,v_4\}$ is contained in $\Span\{v_1,v_2,v_4\}$. Any linear combination of $v_1,v_2,v_4$ is also a linear combination of $v_1,v_2,v_3,v_4$ (with the $v_3$-coefficient equal to zero), so $\Span\{v_1,v_2,v_4\}$ is also contained in $\Span\{v_1,v_2,v_3,v_4\}$, and thus they are equal.

 In the other direction, if we have a linear dependence relation like

$$0 = 2v_1 - \frac 12v_2 + v_3 - 6v_4,$$

 then we can move any nonzero term to the left side of the equation and divide by its coefficient:

$$v_1 = \frac 12\left(\frac 12v_2 - v_3 + 6v_4\right).$$

 This shows that $v_1$ is in $\Span\{v_2,v_3,v_4\}$.

 We leave it to the reader to generalize this proof for any set of vectors.

nodes.title: Increasing Span Criterion
nodes.body: A set of vectors $\{v_1,v_2,\ldots,v_k\}$ is linearly independent if and only if, for every $j$, the vector $v_j$ is not in $\Span\{v_1,v_2,\ldots,v_{j-1}\}$.

nodes.title: Proof: Increasing Span Criterion
nodes.body:
It is equivalent to show that $\{v_1,v_2,\ldots,v_k\}$ is linearly dependent if and only if $v_j$ is in $\Span\{v_1,v_2,\ldots,v_{j-1}\}$ for some $j$. The if implication is an immediate consequence of the previous [linindep-criterion-inspan]. Suppose then that $\{v_1,v_2,\ldots,v_k\}$ is linearly dependent. This means that some $v_j$ is in the span of the others. Choose the largest such $j$. We claim that this $v_j$ is in $\Span\{v_1,v_2,\ldots,v_{j-1}\}$. If not, then

$$v_j = x_1v_1 + x_2v_2 + \cdots + x_{j-1}v_{j-1} + x_{j+1}v_{j+1} + \cdots + x_kv_k$$

 with not all of $x_{j+1},\ldots,x_k$ equal to zero. Suppose for simplicity that $x_k\neq 0$. Then we can rearrange:

$$v_k = -\frac 1{x_k}\bigl( x_1v_1 + x_2v_2 + \cdots + x_{j-1}v_{j-1}
 - v_j + x_{j+1}v_{j+1} + \cdots + x_{p-1}v_{p-1}
 \bigr).$$

 This says that $v_k$ is in the span of $\{v_1,v_2,\ldots,v_{p-1}\}$, which contradicts our assumption that $v_j$ is the last vector in the span of the others.
